Porter County by the numbers

Where is Porter County, Indiana, and how is it laid out?

Porter County sits in the northwest corner of Indiana, on the Chicago side of the state, with Lake Michigan along its northern edge and the Kankakee River along the south. The county seat is Valparaiso, and the two cities are Valparaiso and Portage, which is the largest by both population and land area.

The county covers 521.8 square miles in total. About 418.2 of those are land and 103.6 are water, mostly lake. Nine incorporated towns fill in the map: Beverly Shores, Burns Harbor, Chesterton, Dune Acres, Hebron, Kouts, Ogden Dunes, Porter and Town of Pines. Twelve townships carry the assessment work: Boone, Center, Jackson, Liberty, Morgan, Pine, Pleasant, Portage, Porter, Union, Washington and Westchester.

For a seller this layout matters because a Porter County parcel can sit inside a city, a town, a township only, or a lakeshore community, and each has its own levy mix on the bill. A lake-side house in Ogden Dunes and a farmhouse near Kouts share a county treasurer, yet their tax statements can look very different.

What shaped Porter County's economy and housing?

Steel, a deepwater port and protected dune land shaped the county. The state authorized Porter County in 1835 and it was organized in 1837, named for Captain David Porter, a naval officer of the War of 1812. In 1962 Bethlehem Steel built an integrated mill on the Lake Michigan shore, and the mill, now owned by Cleveland-Cliffs, sits beside the Port of Indiana in Burns Harbor.

Congress created Indiana Dunes National Lakeshore in 1966, and much of the dune country lies in Porter County, including part of Indiana Dunes National Park, Indiana Dunes State Park and the Moraine Nature Preserve. Former hardwood hills farther south were largely cleared for farming.

Getting around depends on U.S. 12, State Route 2 and State Route 49, plus South Shore Line rail stations that link the lakeshore towns toward Chicago. Homes near those stations and the lakefront often draw different buyers than homes in the rural townships, which affects how fast a house moves and what condition problems buyers will tolerate.

Which Porter County office handles which part of a tax bill?

Three offices share the work, and calling the wrong one costs time. The county's own FAQ tells owners to read the TS-1A that comes with the bill first, then sort the question like this:

  • Assessment went up: the Assessor, whose office is at 155 Indiana Ave, Suite 211, Valparaiso, reachable at (219) 465-3460.
  • A deduction dropped off: the Auditor, at (219) 465-3445 or Auditor@porterco.org.
  • Payment posting error: the Treasurer, at (219) 465-3470.
  • Tax rate change: the rate is set at the state level, not by any of the three county offices.

The Assessor's directory lists Sue Neff as county assessor, with a residential real estate supervisor and a director of commercial operations on staff. If you are selling, the Auditor is also where you confirm that a homestead deduction is on file, since a buyer's lender will look at the same record.

How and when do you pay Porter County property tax?

Porter County bills in two installments, spring on May 10 and fall on November 10, and a date that lands on a weekend or holiday moves to the next business day. Bills under $25.00 are not split. Full and partial payments are accepted all year, and penalties apply to late amounts.

A payment is not late if the properly addressed envelope carries a U.S. postmark on or before the due date, or if an express carrier received it by then. The county FAQ points to Indiana Code 6-1.1-37-10 for the penalty rules, and the calculation is printed on the front of the bill.

  • Online through the county's two payment portals, with no extra charge for electronic checks and a processing fee for cards.
  • By phone or mail, with instructions on the county's payment pages. Mail goes to the Treasurer at 155 Indiana Ave, Suite 209, Valparaiso, IN 46383, and the check should not be stapled to the coupon.
  • In person at the Treasurer's office.
  • Through a mortgage, escrow or title company, which has its own electronic portfolio system.

Online payments take at least two days to post, so a payment made this week may still look unpaid on the lookup page. Account history updates nightly. If you overpay, surplus claim forms go out after the June and December settlements, and a spring overpayment is applied to the fall amount.

What does Porter County's tax sale mean for an owner who is behind?

Falling behind can end in an online auction, and the county's 2026 notice shows how it works. The sale was set to begin October 21, 2026 on zeusauction.com, with 533 properties listed and closings starting October 22. To pull a property out of the sale, the Treasurer had to receive cash or certified funds at 155 Indiana Avenue, Suite 209 by noon on October 20, 2026.

An owner whose property is sold can still redeem it. The notice sets the redemption price at 110 percent of the minimum bid within six months and 115 percent after that, plus any overbid and 5 percent annual interest on it, plus later taxes the buyer paid. For certificates sold in the 2026 sale, the redemption period runs to Friday, October 22, 2027. If a property sells above the minimum bid and is not redeemed, the former owner of record may be entitled to the surplus.

The county's page on certified properties adds that some taxpayers may qualify for a tax sale payment plan, and that a property not sold but pursued for title carries a 120 day redemption window. Redemption questions go to the Auditor at (219) 465-3449, and payment-plan questions to the Treasurer at taxquestions@porterco.org.

How does a property tax appeal work in Porter County?

An appeal starts with Form 130, filed with the assessing official, and the county Assessor handles it where no township assessor exists. Use one form per parcel. For a current-year assessment, the form is due by June 15 of the assessment year if the notice was mailed before May 1, and by June 15 of the year the tax statements go out if it was mailed on or after May 1.

A separate limited error correction route allows a filing within three years after the taxes were first due. Evidence is not required on filing, but both sides exchange what they have at a preliminary informal meeting.

  • If the meeting fails, the county Property Tax Assessment Board of Appeals must hold a hearing within 180 days of filing, with at least 30 days of notice to you.
  • You may then take the result to the Indiana Board of Tax Review on Form 131 within 45 days.
  • After that, the Indiana Tax Court, again within 45 days of the board's final decision.

How do Indiana's caps and recent changes affect a Porter County bill?

Indiana limits what an owner pays as a share of gross assessed value: 1 percent for a homestead that has the standard deduction, 2 percent for other residential and agricultural land, and 3 percent for nonresidential and personal property. The Department of Local Government Finance gives a sample: a $100,000 homestead capped at $1,000 whose liability is $2,100 gets a $1,100 circuit breaker credit.

The 2025 reform known as SEA 1 is changing the deduction mix. An analysis published by the Indiana Capital Chronicle describes the $48,000 standard deduction stepping down each year after 2026 and ending in 2031, while the supplemental deduction rises, and a new homestead credit of 10 percent of the bill up to $300 begins in 2026. Check your own statement, since the effect varies by home value.

What should you settle before selling a Porter County house with tax due?

Start by getting the parcel's balance from the Treasurer, then decide how it will be paid at closing. A title company will want unpaid taxes settled at closing, and a property already on the certified list needs the redemption amount rather than the base tax.

  • Pull the bill and the lookup balance, and check whether a spring or fall installment is still open.
  • Ask the Auditor whether any deduction on the parcel will lapse after the sale.
  • If the house is on the tax sale list, ask about the redemption figure and the payment plan.
  • Tell the title company about any open appeal.

Because bills come in two installments, a sale between due dates can leave one installment open. Ask the title company how that amount will be split at closing.

More questions about Porter County, IN Property Tax Guide

What are the Porter County property tax due dates?

Spring is due May 10 and fall is due November 10. If either date falls on a weekend or holiday, it moves to the next business day, and a postmark on or before the date counts as on time.

Where do I mail a Porter County tax payment?

Mail it with the coupon to the Treasurer at 155 Indiana Ave, Suite 209, Valparaiso, IN 46383. The county asks that the check not be stapled or clipped to the coupon, and a self-addressed stamped envelope gets you a receipt in about six to eight weeks.

Who do I call about a higher assessment in Porter County?

Call the Assessor at (219) 465-3460. Call the Auditor at (219) 465-3445 if a deduction dropped, and the Treasurer at (219) 465-3470 if a payment posted wrong.

Can I sell a Porter County house that is on the tax sale list?

Yes, but the delinquent taxes and costs have to be cleared before the sale or redeemed afterward. Ask the Treasurer for the payoff and the Auditor for the redemption amount, then have the title company include it in the closing statement.

How long do I have to appeal an assessment in Porter County?

For a current-year assessment, Form 130 is generally due by June 15, depending on when the notice was mailed. A limited error correction can be filed within three years after the taxes were first due.

Marion County by the numbers

Where is Marion County, Indiana, and how is it organized?

Marion County sits in central Indiana, and its seat is Indianapolis, which is also the state capital. The county covers 403.01 square miles, of which 396.30 are land and 6.71 are water (Wikipedia).

The county was founded on April 1, 1822, and the state capital moved to Indianapolis from Corydon on January 10, 1825. Nine townships make up the map in a three by three grid: Pike, Washington and Lawrence across the top, Wayne, Center and Warren through the middle, and Decatur, Perry and Franklin along the bottom.

City and county government merged in 1970 under a plan known as Unigov. Four places stayed outside it as excluded municipalities: Beech Grove, Lawrence, Southport and the town of Speedway. Several small included towns, such as Clermont, Homecroft and Williams Creek, keep limited local authority. School districts and fire districts were never merged into the consolidated government.

For an owner this matters because a Marion County tax bill can carry levies from more than one layer of local government, depending on which township, school district and municipality the parcel sits in.

What does Marion County property tax cost and who sets it?

Marion County does not have a single flat rate. Each parcel sits in a taxing district, and the district rate is applied to the assessed value after deductions and credits. The Treasurer publishes a "Review Tax Rates" page on indy.gov where you can look up the rate for a given year.

Three separate bodies touch your bill:

  • The Marion County Assessor sets assessed values and takes appeals.
  • The Marion County Auditor handles homestead and other deductions. The Recorder's deed page points owners to the Auditor for the standard homestead and mortgage deductions.
  • The Marion County Treasurer bills, collects and distributes the money.

Indiana changed the homestead rules in 2025. According to a May 2026 memo from the Department of Local Government Finance, the standard homestead deduction is $40,000 for the 2026 assessment date, down from $48,000, and it steps down by $10,000 each year until it ends with the 2030 assessment date. The supplemental deduction percentage rises over the same period, to 46 percent for taxes payable in 2027. A Purdue Extension summary adds a new supplemental homestead credit of 10 percent of the bill, up to $300, starting in 2026.

If you are selling, these changes mostly affect the buyer. A new owner has to file for their own homestead deduction after closing, so the bill you paid may not match the bill they receive.

What are the key Marion County property tax dates and offices?

Marion County property tax is due May 11 and November 10 in 2026, and payments go to the Treasurer's Office in the City-County Building. The table below lists the facts the county publishes.

The Treasurer's Office says owners can pay online, by phone, by mail, in person or at a bank, and can schedule recurring payments through an account login. Paperless statements are also available.

How do penalties work if a Marion County bill is paid late?

A late payment adds 5 percent of the unpaid tax if you pay within 30 days of the due date and have no prior-year balance on the parcel. If the tax and penalty are not paid within those 30 days, the penalty becomes 10 percent (Indiana DLGF).

A short delay can therefore cost real money on a larger bill. On a $3,000 half-year installment, 5 percent is $150 and 10 percent is $300.

Past a certain point the county can place the parcel in a tax sale. Marion County places a lien on homes with unpaid taxes and auctions the lien online. The 2026 sale ran October 13 through 16. To stop a parcel from being sold, an owner had to pay all unpaid taxes, penalties and special assessments, solid waste and stormwater fees, plus a $325 tax sale administration fee, by October 8, 2026 at 4:30 PM. The county accepts cash, certified checks, cashier's checks or money orders for that payment, and does not take personal or business checks.

The Treasurer's site lists a tax sale payment plan, partial payments and paying after a sale as separate topics, so ask the office what applies to your parcel.

How do you appeal a Marion County assessment?

You file a written appeal, Form 130, with the assessing official, which in Marion County is the Assessor. Under the state's November 2025 fact sheet, the deadline is June 15 of the year the tax bill is mailed when the county sent the notice of assessment after May 1, and June 15 of the assessment year when it sent the notice earlier.

After filing, the Assessor holds an informal meeting. If that does not settle it, the Property Tax Assessment Board of Appeals must hold a hearing within 180 days of the petition. A further appeal goes to the Indiana Board of Tax Review on Form 131.

A pending appeal can lower what you owe in the meantime. The state fact sheet says you may pay based on the prior year's assessment while the appeal is pending, without penalty. A law firm note from April 2026 says Indiana Code 6-1.1-15-10 applies this rule and recommends sending the Treasurer a written explanation with the payment. The difference is not erased, though. If the appeal fails, you owe it.

Recent assessment activity in Marion County has been heavy. The same law firm reported that the Assessor added nearly $5.5 billion of assessed value to Indianapolis commercial and industrial property for the January 1, 2025 assessment date.

The Assessor also posted a notice that owners hurt by recent flooding may ask for a review by submitting Form 137R, and a disaster reassessment petition is listed among its services.

What happens to the tax bill when you sell a house in Marion County?

The seller owes the taxes for the period they owned the house, and the title company usually settles this at closing. Indiana taxes are paid after the year they cover, so a spring or fall installment can still be unpaid on closing day.

Before listing or accepting an offer, it helps to gather these items:

  • The latest tax statement and the parcel number.
  • Proof that the last installment was paid, or the amount still owed.
  • Any pending Form 130 appeal, since it changes what the bill should be.
  • Notice of any tax sale list status, which the Treasurer can confirm.

The transfer itself runs through the Assessor first. Deeds and sales disclosures must be stamped at Room W121, with a $10 transfer fee per parcel and $20 per sales disclosure form, and then the stamped deed goes to the Recorder, where the fee is $35 per document (indy.gov). The Assessor asks owners to build the sales disclosure in the Properly online system.

A house with back taxes, a lien or a stalled estate can be hard to sell on the open market. Marion County owners in that position often look at selling as-is so that the unpaid amount is taken from the sale price rather than paid up front.

What is the climate and economy like in Marion County?

Marion County has hot summers and cold winters, so roofs, gutters and heating systems get a full workout. Recent January averages sit near 20 degrees Fahrenheit and July near 86. The record low is minus 22 (January 1985) and the record high is 104 (June 1988). Monthly precipitation runs from about 2.05 inches in January to 4.78 inches in July (Wikipedia).

The county economy is large. Wikipedia reports a total GDP of $135.593 billion for 2024. Indianapolis International Airport and Eagle Creek Airpark are both in the county.

The median home here was built in 1972, per the Census figures already shown above, so many houses are past the age where roofs, furnaces and sewer lines need replacing. Condition is a common reason owners decide to sell as-is instead of repairing.

When is the next Marion County property tax due?

The Marion County Treasurer lists two 2026 due dates: May 11 and November 10. The office will have extended hours of 8 AM to 5:30 PM on November 6, 9 and 10, and it is closed on November 3 and November 11.

Where do I pay Marion County property tax in person?

Go to the Treasurer's Office in the City-County Building, 200 E. Washington St., Suite 1001, Indianapolis. Regular hours are 8 AM to 4:30 PM, Monday to Friday. You can also call (317) 327-4444.

How late can I file a Marion County assessment appeal?

The state's fact sheet gives June 15 as the filing deadline for Form 130, tied to the year the tax bill is mailed or the assessment year, depending on when the notice went out. Confirm the date for your notice with the Assessor at (317) 327-4907.

Can I stop a Marion County tax sale?

Yes, before the sale. For 2026 the owner had to pay all unpaid taxes, penalties, special assessments, solid waste and stormwater fees and a $325 administration fee by October 8, 2026 at 4:30 PM. Contact the Treasurer for what applies after that date.

Who stamps a deed in Marion County before it is recorded?

The Marion County Assessor does, in Room W121 of the City-County Building. The stamped deed then goes to the Recorder's Office. Fees at the Assessor are $10 per parcel and $20 for a sales disclosure when one is required.

Do I owe property tax if the house sells before the bill arrives?

Usually the sellers' share is settled at closing through the title company, since Indiana bills in arrears. Ask the title company to confirm both installments for the parcel and any amounts still open.

Hamilton County by the numbers

Where is Hamilton County and how fast has it grown?

Hamilton County lies directly north of Indianapolis, with Noblesville as the county seat. It covers about 402 square miles and borders Tipton, Madison, Hancock, Marion, Boone and Clinton counties. The northern part is still largely farmland, and suburban development has spread north from Indianapolis since World War II.

Carmel is the largest city and ranked fifth in the state in 2020. Fishers ranked sixth and Noblesville twelfth. Arcadia, Atlanta, Cicero, Sheridan and Westfield are towns. The county has nine townships, and Clay Township matches the boundaries of Carmel.

The land passed to the United States in the 1818 Treaty of St. Mary's, and the county was set up in 1823 and named for Alexander Hamilton. Geist and Morse reservoirs are two man-made lakes that add waterfront living to the housing mix.

What drives the Hamilton County economy?

A state-run employer list for Hamilton County, drawn from a commercial directory, ranks CNO Financial Group, Bankers Conseco Life, RCI, Navient, Roche Diagnostics, Openlane, CAPE, King Systems, the Noblesville Walmart Supercenter and Freedom Mortgage as the top ten. The names lean toward insurance, lending and diagnostics, and the list shows no employee counts.

A 2023 Indianapolis Business Journal retrospective adds detail on the growth:

  • Carmel is home to nearly 130 corporate or regional headquarters, including CNO Financial Group, KAR Auction Services and Allegion.
  • Fishers houses Navient and Roche Diagnostics, two of the county's largest employers.
  • Westfield's Grand Park Sports Campus covers more than 400 acres and opened in 2014.
  • Deer Creek Music Center, now Ruoff Music Center, opened in Noblesville in 1989.
  • From 2000 to 2015, county household income rose 21% while rental costs rose 51%.

The county's assessors expected 2025 residential values to rise, which is why the cap and appeal rules below matter.

Which offices handle property tax in Hamilton County?

The treasurer collects payments, the auditor handles deductions and the tax sale, and the assessor values property. The treasurer and auditor work from the Historic Courthouse in downtown Noblesville.

OfficeDetails
Treasurer33 N 9th Street, Suite 112, Noblesville; 317-776-9620; Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
Auditor deductions desk33 N 9th Street, first floor, southwest corner; 317-770-4412
Auditor tax sale desk33 N 9th Street, Suite 214; tax.sale@hamiltoncounty.in.gov

The county accepts payments online, by mail, in person and at listed banks. Credit cards work only online. Mail must carry a postmark by the due date, and a postage meter date does not count. A drop box sits at the west doors of the Historic Courthouse, and anything left after midnight on the deadline counts as late. Banks that take payments include BMO Bank, Community First Bank of Indiana, Farmers Bank, First Farmers Bank, Horizon Bank, Merchants Bank of Indiana and Star Financial Bank. Bring the tax statement.

The county also offers e-billing and an online portal where owners can see statements, payments, assessed values and property record cards.

How does Hamilton County assess so many homes?

Hamilton County had 148,707 parcels at the end of 2024, and the assessor's office does most of the valuation work in house. The 2025 ratio study narrative gives a clear view of the pace of change.

For 2025, the state's new cost tables, adjusted by a Verified Economic Modifier, significantly affected improvement values. Smaller neighborhoods with little sales data had lagged the market, so some saw large increases, while larger neighborhoods saw little change. The county expected 2025 residential assessments to rise. The study also cites MIBOR statistics showing a 7.2% increase in median single-family sale price from January 2024 to January 2025.

The 2024 cyclical phase reviewed residential property in Washington Township and parts of Noblesville and Fall Creek townships, along with agricultural land in White River, Wayne and Delaware townships. Reviewed commercial neighborhoods included hotels, car dealerships, self-storage and the major downtown redevelopment. When a permit is pulled for an addition or remodel, the property is inspected. Transitional areas where older homes are replaced by new construction may get their own neighborhoods.

How do I appeal an assessment or lower the bill in Hamilton County?

File a Form 130 with the assessor, one per parcel, by June 15. The year depends on whether the Form 11 notice was mailed before May 1. The assessor holds an informal meeting, and then the county appeals board must hold a hearing within 180 days with 30 days of written notice. A $50 penalty can apply for a no-show with no continuance. If you disagree, Form 131 goes to the Indiana Board of Tax Review.

The state also caps the bill at 1% of gross assessed value for a homestead, 2% for other residential and farmland, and 3% for nonresidential and personal property. You need the homestead deduction for the 1% cap. The county's deduction page lists the standard homestead deduction, the over 65 credit, the blind and disabled credit and recorded land contract benefits. It asks owners to file by January 15 to affect the next bill, and once approved you generally do not reapply unless you change the deed, marry or change the property's use. A third-party vendor, Tax Management Associates, may mail letters asking homeowners to clarify eligibility, and the county says those letters are legitimate.

What happens at the Hamilton County tax sale?

The 2026 Hamilton County real property tax sale was set for Thursday, October 8, 2026 at 10 a.m. in the Second Floor Historic Courtroom at 33 North 9th Street. The auditor runs it and payments go to the treasurer.

  • To pull a parcel from the sale, pay the full amount to the treasurer by noon the day before the sale, in cash, cashier's check or money order.
  • The property list is updated each Friday, normally by noon, in the two months before the sale.
  • An owner has three years after a sale to claim surplus funds if the parcel sold for more than the debt.

State law adds penalties before a sale. A late payment takes 5% if made within 30 days and no earlier delinquency exists, and 10% in other cases. An extra 10% of unpaid tax is added after later installment dates. A sale through a title company clears the amount from the seller's proceeds.

What should Hamilton County sellers know about schools and neighborhoods?

The county's school corporations and cities shape how buyers search. Clay Terrace, a 577,000-square-foot open-air mall in Carmel, opened in 2004, and the Carmel Center for the Performing Arts includes a 1,600-seat hall. Fishers added about 2,200 homes with its 2010 annexation of the Geist area, and Westfield's U.S. 31 conversion brought state and private investment.

Older areas near downtown Noblesville and Carmel sit beside new construction, so condition varies by block.

More questions about Hamilton County, IN Property Tax Guide

Who do I pay property tax to in Hamilton County?

You pay the Hamilton County Treasurer at 33 N 9th Street, Suite 112 in Noblesville, or online. The phone number is 317-776-9620. Credit cards are accepted online only.

Can I sell a flood-damaged house in Hamilton County?

Yes. Many owners sell as-is after a flood. Buyers will ask for photos, insurance claims and repair records, and standard homeowners policies generally exclude flood damage, so check your coverage first.

When is the appeal deadline in Hamilton County?

June 15, filed on Form 130 with the county assessor. The year depends on whether the Form 11 notice came before or after May 1.

What if my Hamilton County parcel is on the tax sale list?

You can remove it by paying the full balance to the treasurer by noon the day before the sale, using certified funds. The list is searchable on the county site and updated on Fridays.

Do I lose my homestead deduction when I sell?

The deduction belongs to the owner who files for it, so the buyer files a new application. The county page asks owners to file by January 15 to affect the next bill, and it says you generally do not need to reapply unless the deed, marital status or use changes.

St Joseph County by the numbers

What is St. Joseph County, Indiana, and where does it sit?

St. Joseph County is in north central Indiana along the Michigan line, with South Bend as its county seat and largest city. The county was formed in 1830, when it had 287 residents, and takes its name from the St. Joseph River, which flows through it on the way to Lake Michigan.

It covers 461 square miles, of which about 3.5 are water. Berrien and Cass counties in Michigan lie to the north, Elkhart County to the east, Marshall and Starke counties to the south and LaPorte County to the west. Mishawaka is the other large city, and the county is part of the Michiana region and the South Bend-Mishawaka metro area.

The 2020 census counted 272,912 residents, the fifth-highest total of any Indiana county. The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 272,861, so the population has been close to flat since 2020.

What do the Census numbers say about homes and owners in St. Joseph County?

About 69% of St. Joseph County homes are owner-occupied, and the median value of those homes is $192,800 in the 2020 to 2024 survey. The county has 119,768 housing units by the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate and issued 611 building permits in 2025.

Which towns and employers make up the county economy?

South Bend and Mishawaka anchor the county, and the Census Bureau counted 5,959 employer establishments and 120,211 jobs in 2023. Employment changed by minus 0.1% from 2022 to 2023.

  • Health care and social assistance receipts reached about $2.74 billion in 2022.

About 33.5% of adults 25 and older hold a bachelor's degree or higher, well above Wayne County's 20.5%. Mean travel time to work is 21.1 minutes.

For a property owner, the assessment on your own parcel matters most. The county assessor values each parcel, the county treasurer collects, and Indiana bills combine county, city and school levies.

How does the St. Joseph County assessment and appeal process work?

The St. Joseph County Assessor values every parcel, and the owner can appeal with Indiana's Form 130. The assessor in 2026 is Michael Castellon, and the office is in the County-City Building.

Indiana's Department of Local Government Finance describes the steps:

  • File Form 130 by June 15. If the county mailed the notice of assessment before May 1, that is June 15 of the assessment year. Otherwise it is June 15 of the year the treasurer mails the bill.
  • File a separate petition for each parcel.
  • The county's property tax assessment board of appeals, known as the PTABOA, must hold a hearing within 180 days of filing, with at least 30 days' notice.
  • If you disagree with the result, file Form 131 with the Indiana Board of Tax Review. You can also go there if the PTABOA has not ruled in 180 days.
  • A no-show without a granted continuance or timely withdrawal can bring a $50 penalty.

The last determined assessment is presumed correct. If the assessment rose by more than 5% over the prior date, the assessor has the burden of proof, unless the increase comes from improvements or a change in use.

What happened with St. Joseph County assessments in 2025 and 2026?

The 2025 cycle produced nearly 14,000 appeals in St. Joseph County, and the 2026 cycle is expected to produce far fewer. ABC57 reported on May 12, 2026 that Castellon announced a countywide average decrease of 4%, with about 86% of the county seeing a lower assessed value.

The 2026 notices began arriving about April 27. By the Friday before that report only 394 appeals had been filed, against about 8,600 at the same point a year earlier, and Castellon forecast fewer than 1,500 for the year. The reported deadline was June 15, 2026.

The office also changed how it values property. It created submarkets for long-time owners in places such as Notre Dame and New Carlisle so they are not compared to new construction, valued land by square footage rather than lot type, and applied a 20/80 rule that assigns 20% of value to land and 80% to improvements.

One resident's five-acre lot bought for $9,000 in 2012 saw its land value rise from $14,900 to $57,700 before the owner appealed. The assessor later lowered it to nearly $11,000. The case shows that an appeal can succeed when the numbers do not match the facts.

When are St. Joseph County property taxes due, and what happens if you pay late?

Property tax in St. Joseph County is due twice a year: May 11 and November 10 in 2026. The county mails one bill that includes both installments, and the payment goes to the county treasurer.

Indiana's Department of Local Government Finance sets the penalty. A late payment with no back taxes owed on the same property gets a 5% penalty if paid within 30 days of the due date. If the tax and penalty remain unpaid after 30 days, the penalty rises to 10%.

A parcel that stays delinquent can end up in a county tax sale. The county treasurer can tell you what is owed. If you plan to sell, ask them for a payoff before the closing date.

How do property taxes work when you sell a house in St. Joseph County?

When you sell, the title company confirms what is owed and pays it from your proceeds. Ask it how the current-year bill is divided between you and the buyer, because the split depends on the purchase agreement.

  • Ask the treasurer's office whether any installment is unpaid or delinquent.
  • Check the assessed value on the notice and decide whether an appeal is still open.
  • Look for liens or open permits that the title search might turn up.
  • Keep the Form 11 notice and your tax bills with your closing papers.

We buy houses in St. Joseph County as-is, including houses with back taxes, tenants or repairs. The title company handles the title and recording steps, and the offer is yours to accept or decline.

Why should owners in the county check their notice every year?

Assessments in St. Joseph County swung sharply between 2025 and 2026, so a notice you ignored last year may now be wrong in the other direction. A drop does not always show up as lower tax, because the bill also depends on rates set by local governments.

The assessor's office held town halls ahead of the 2026 notices, including a May 16 session at the St. Joseph County Public Library and a June 13 session at the Mishawaka-Penn-Harris Library. Those events are a way to ask staff how the new submarkets were drawn.

If you are selling soon, a lower assessment helps a buyer's carrying costs, and a higher one may be worth challenging before you list.

File Indiana Form 130 with the county assessor, one form per parcel, by June 15 of the right year. A PTABOA hearing follows within 180 days.

Yes. The title company pays what is owed from the proceeds at closing, so ask the treasurer for a payoff figure before the closing date.

Allen County by the numbers

Which county bills property tax in Fort Wayne and the rest of Allen County?

Allen County, Indiana bills it, and the county treasurer collects. Fort Wayne is the county seat, but the tax bill for a house in Grabill, Huntertown, Leo-Cedarville or Monroeville comes from the same county offices.

The county covers 660.02 square miles in northeast Indiana, which makes it the largest county in the state by area, and it holds 20 townships. Its population was 385,410 in 2020 and is estimated at 402,329 for 2025. About 67.6% of occupied housing units were owner-occupied in 2020.

Four public school districts serve the county: East Allen, Fort Wayne Community Schools, Northwest Allen and Southwest Allen. Fort Wayne Community Schools is the largest district in Indiana.

Why do the three rivers matter for a house in Fort Wayne?

The St. Joseph, St. Marys and Maumee rivers meet in Fort Wayne, and the city has a long flood history. The 1913 flood killed seven people, left about 15,000 homeless and damaged more than 5,500 buildings.

In 1982 about 9,000 residents had to leave, around 2,000 buildings were damaged and the loss was $56.1 million. A $50 million flood control project later centered on Headwaters Park.

If your Allen County house is near a river or low ground, confirm its flood zone status with your insurer or the city before you list it.

What is the weather like, and what has it done to local homes?

Fort Wayne has four distinct seasons, with a January low near 16 degrees and a July high near 84. Precipitation runs from about 38 to 39 inches a year, and the city sees roughly 39 thunderstorm days.

The June 2012 derecho is the storm that most owners remember. Wind gusts reached 91 mph, 78,000 customers lost power, about 500 trees came down and the damage was put at $2.5 million. An EF1 tornado also hit a northeast-side shopping center in May 2001 and injured three people.

  • Record low: minus 24 degrees, set January 12, 1918.

Storm damage to a roof, siding or trees is easy to see in an inspection, and an as-is sale means you do not have to fix it first.

Other large employers include Parkview Health, Amazon, Lutheran Health Network, Lincoln Financial Group and BFGoodrich. Steel Dynamics is the only Fortune 500 company headquartered in the city.

Allen County's unemployment rate was 3.4% in 2025 with a labor force of 204,024, and the first phase of a Google data center was completed in December 2025.

How do you get around Allen County?

Interstate 69 is the only interstate through Fort Wayne, and I-469 is an auxiliary beltway that was built from 1988 to 1995. Four U.S. routes cross the city: 24, 27, 30 and 33. State roads 1, 3, 14, 37 and 930 also meet there.

Fort Wayne International Airport has direct service from five airlines to 13 domestic destinations. Higher education includes Indiana University Fort Wayne, Purdue University Fort Wayne, Indiana Tech and the University of Saint Francis.

Locals describe the city by quadrant: northeast, northwest, southeast and southwest. Calhoun Street divides the south side, and the St. Joseph and Maumee rivers divide the north and east.

When are Allen County taxes due, and what are the penalties?

Taxes are due in two installments, May 10 and November 10. Indiana's Department of Local Government Finance lists a 5% penalty if you pay within 30 days after a due date and have no back taxes on the property. After those 30 days, or if prior taxes are unpaid, the penalty is 10%.

In 2025 the fall deadline was Monday, November 10, and payments had to be received or postmarked by then. If a due date lands on a weekend, check the treasurer's notice for the shifted date.

If you appeal an assessment, Indiana lets you pay on the previous year's assessment while the appeal is pending, without penalty.

How much can an Indiana tax bill rise?

The 1% homestead cap applies only if the owner receives the homestead standard deduction. A house you rent out or that sits empty is generally in the 2% class instead, so the applicable cap on an inherited house rises from 1% to 2% once homestead status ends.

How do you appeal an Allen County assessment?

File Form 130 with the assessing official, one petition per parcel, by June 15 of the assessment year if the county mailed the notice before May 1. When the notice is mailed on or after May 1, the deadline is June 15 of the year the tax bill is mailed.

  • An informal meeting follows, where both sides trade evidence.
  • The county board (PTABOA) must hold a hearing within 180 days of filing and mail notice at least 30 days before.
  • If you still disagree, or the board does not rule in 180 days, file Form 131 with the Indiana Board of Tax Review.
  • Tax Court and the Indiana Supreme Court are the next levels.

The assessment is presumed correct. A recent sale of your home, comparable sales, a purchase offer or an appraisal all count as evidence. The assessor has the burden of proof if the assessment rose more than 5% over the prior date, unless the rise reflects renovation or a change of use or zoning. A missed hearing can cost a $50 penalty.

  • Confirm whether a lender escrow account paid the last installment.
  • Ask the assessor to review any recent value increase of more than 5%.
  • Keep the homestead deduction in mind if you move out before the sale.

File Form 130 by June 15 when the county mailed the assessment notice before May 1 of the assessment year. If the notice came after May 1, the deadline is June 15 of the year the tax bill is mailed.

How much can my Allen County property tax go up?

Indiana's circuit breaker caps are 1% for a homestead, 2% for other residential property and agricultural land, and 3% for nonresidential property and personal property. The homestead cap requires the homestead standard deduction.

Yes. Ask the treasurer or title company for the payoff, and the amount can be paid from the sale proceeds at closing. We buy Allen County houses as-is, and a tax balance does not stop us from making an offer.

Lake County by the numbers

Where is Lake County, Indiana, and how big is it?

Lake County is the Indiana county in the far northwest corner of the state, on the Lake Michigan shore and inside the Chicago metro area. Crown Point is the county seat. The county covers 626.5 square miles, of which 498.9 is land and 127.6 is water, which gives it more water area than any of Indiana's 92 counties.

Lake County was established on February 16, 1837. Its land is flat in the north and south, with the Valparaiso Moraine rising through the middle. The lowest point is 585 feet on the lake shoreline and the highest is 801 feet in northeastern Winfield Township. Porter County lies to the east, Jasper and Newton counties to the south, and Cook, Will and Kankakee counties in Illinois to the west.

The county has 19 incorporated places. Hammond is the largest by population at 77,879, and Gary is the largest by area. Calumet Township is the most populous township, with 91,970 residents in 2020.

How did steel shape Lake County's economy and housing?

Heavy industry built most of Lake County's older neighborhoods. Inland Steel opened a plant in East Chicago in 1903, and U.S. Steel founded Gary Works in 1906. Population climbed from 37,892 in 1900 to 261,310 in 1930 and peaked at 546,253 in 1970.

Steel employment topped 60,000 in the 1960s and fell to about 18,000 by 2015. The 2020 census count of 498,700 is well below that peak. Gary Works employed over 30,000 people in 1970 and 2,246 in 2023, and Gary's 2020 census found 23.2% of its housing units vacant.

Industry still matters. The employers Wikipedia lists include U.S. Steel Gary Works, Cleveland-Cliffs Indiana Harbor Works in East Chicago, the BP Whiting Refinery, Canadian National Railway and Unilever in Whiting, Cargill in Hammond and NiSource in Merrillville. In 2010, manufacturing was the largest employment sector at over 45,000 workers, followed by health care and social assistance at 44,000 and public administration at 40,000.

The result is a county with very different housing stock from one block to the next. Gary's vacancy rate and Crown Point's steady growth sit in the same county and on the same tax rolls. Owners of inherited or damaged houses in the older parts of the county are often the ones who ask about as-is sales.

What is each Lake County city known for?

  • Hammond: 77,879 residents in 2020, an industrial city that borders Chicago and Lake Michigan. The School City of Hammond runs 11 elementary schools, two middle schools and two high schools.
  • Gary: 69,093 residents in 2020, down from 178,320 in 1960. It is the western gateway to Indiana Dunes National Park and has Gary/Chicago International Airport.
  • Crown Point: 33,899 residents in 2020. Center Township is served by Crown Point Community School Corporation and Ross Township by Merrillville Community School Corporation. The Lake County Fair is held there each August.

The Lake County school district a house sits in feeds directly into its tax rate, which is why the same assessed value can produce different bills in Hammond, Gary and Crown Point.

What is the weather in Lake County, and what does it do to a house?

Lake County has cold, snowy winters and warm summers. At the Lowell weather station, normals from 1981 to 2010 show 39.46 inches of precipitation and 29.3 inches of snow a year, with a January average low of 14.4 degrees and a July average high of 83.8 degrees. The record low is minus 29 in December 1989 and the record high is 104 in June 1988.

Lake-effect snow adds to winter totals near the shore, and thunderstorms occur on about 40 to 50 days a year. Freeze and thaw cycles are hard on roofs, gutters and old plumbing, and houses with deferred maintenance tend to show it. A cash sale lets the owner skip repairs that a mortgage buyer might demand.

How do roads and trains connect Lake County?

Interstate 65 runs north and south through the county, and the Frank Borman Expressway (I-80/94 with US 6) links the Illinois line to the Indiana Toll Road. US 30 follows the old Lincoln Highway, US 12 east of Gary is the Dunes Highway, and Broadway (IN 53) and Cline Avenue (IN 912) fill in the grid.

The South Shore Line commuter rail serves the county, and the Munster/Dyer station opened on March 31, 2026. About 44,000 workers commuted from Lake County to Chicago in 2007.

Which Lake County office do I contact about property tax?

The county treasurer has three counter locations, each open Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The Auditor's office is in the Crown Point government building.

For 2026, the state lists no Form 11 mailing in Calumet, Center, Hobart, Ross and St. John townships, and it shows a June 15, 2027 appeal deadline for them. That is a year later than the June 15, 2026 deadline listed for LaPorte County.

Each of those townships has its own assessor line: Calumet (219) 885-0555, Center (219) 663-0841, Hobart (219) 942-7878, Ross (219) 769-7667 and St. John (219) 365-2777. If your house is in another Lake County township, call the county number to find out which notice applies. When no Form 11 is sent, the state says the tax bill serves as the notice.

How does Indiana's 2025 property tax law affect Lake County owners?

Homestead owners in Lake County get a $48,000 standard deduction on taxes payable in 2026, which drops to $40,000 for 2027 and $30,000 for 2028. In exchange, the supplemental deduction rises from 40% to 46% to 52% over the same years. A new credit gives homesteads that qualify for the standard deduction the lesser of 10% of their liability or $300 without an application.

The old over-65 deduction became a credit of up to $150, with income limits of $60,000 single and $70,000 joint. Caps stay at 1% of gross assessed value for homesteads, 2% for other residential and farm land, and 3% for other property. Lake County's Auditor links to an online deduction filing page for these claims.

What is the Lake County tax sale and can an owner stop it?

Yes, an owner can stop a sale, but only by paying before the deadline. The 2026 Lake County tax sale ran online at zeusauction.com beginning at 5:30 p.m. on September 4, 2026, and properties started closing in batches on September 7.

  • To pull a parcel from the sale, the Treasurer had to receive the amount due by 4:30 p.m. on September 4, in cash or certified funds
  • Postmarks did not count, and payment had to arrive by mail or in person at 2293 N. Main Street
  • The minimum bid covered delinquent taxes, special assessments, current-year taxes, penalties and a $50 postage and publication amount, plus other sale costs
  • Owners of record may have a right to surplus if a parcel sold above the minimum bid and is not redeemed

Redemption for certificates sold in 2026 expires September 8, 2027. The cost is 110% of the minimum bid within six months of the sale and 115% after that, plus any excess bid with 5% annual interest. Anyone who owns a parcel that sold should read the county's tax sale notice now.

Taxes are paid in two installments, with the state listing May 11 and November 10 for 2026, and a payment made within 30 days late, by an owner with no earlier delinquency, carries a 5% penalty while later payment costs 10%. A seller who is behind can sell before a sale is scheduled and have the balance paid from the closing proceeds.

Appeals follow the state path. File Form 130 with the assessing official, expect an informal meeting, and then a hearing by the county board within 180 days. If you disagree, Form 131 goes to the Indiana Board of Tax Review. Only the current assessment can be appealed this way, and evidence can be a sale, comparable sales or an appraisal.

You can pay at the Treasurer's offices in Crown Point, Hammond or Gary, open Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

Not in every township. The state shows no Form 11 mailed for Calumet, Center, Hobart, Ross and St. John, with a June 15, 2027 appeal date.

Check the Treasurer's tax sale list, or call 219-755-3760. The county posts its notice, parcel list and eligibility details on the Treasurer's page.

Madison County by the numbers

Where is Madison County, Indiana, and what is it like?

Madison County is in east central Indiana, and its seat is the city of Anderson. The county covers 452.90 square miles, almost all of it land, and its neighbors are Grant, Delaware, Henry, Hancock, Hamilton and Tipton counties (Wikipedia).

The state authorized the county on January 4, 1823 and named it for James Madison. Pendleton was the first settlement to carry the county name, but it sat off center, so the seat moved to Anderson. Anderson was platted in 1827, the move began in 1828 and was complete by 1836. The first courthouse was finished in 1832.

The land is nearly flat, with some hills along the White River and Fall Creek. The West Branch of the White River crosses the lower middle of the county, and Fall Creek runs through the south. Besides Anderson, the county has the city of Alexandria and part of Elwood, along with communities such as Ovid and Edgewood Village.

The 2020 census counted 130,129 people in the county and 54,788 in Anderson.

What drives the Madison County economy?

Madison County grew up on manufacturing, and Anderson is still defined by it. Natural gas was found at Anderson and Alexandria in 1887, and free gas drew glass makers and other factories. The gas ran out around 1912, and some plants left.

Delco Remy and Guide Lamp became the city's two leading employers for decades. Wikipedia reports General Motors employed nearly 22,000 people in Anderson in the 1970s and fewer than 2,600 by 2006.

A February 2019 list of the largest employers in Anderson, as reported on Wikipedia, shows how the base has shifted toward health care and services:

Anderson is also the world headquarters of the Church of God and home to Anderson University, and Mounds State Park sits against the city's eastern edge.

How do you get around Madison County?

Interstate 69 is the main route, and it crosses the southeast corner of Anderson with an exit at State Road 9 and State Road 109 (Exit 226). From there it runs about 40 miles southwest to Indianapolis and 83 miles northeast to Fort Wayne.

State Road 32 runs east and west through the center of Anderson along 14th Street, reaching Muncie 19 miles east and Noblesville 19 miles west. State Road 9 follows Scatterfield Road on the east side, with Alexandria 11 miles north and Pendleton 10 miles southwest.

Schools follow district lines that do not match city lines. Most of Anderson falls in Anderson Community School Corporation, a small part is in South Madison Community School Corporation, and Anderson Preparatory Academy is a tuition-free public charter school.

Who handles Madison County property tax, and where are the offices?

Property tax in Madison County runs through three offices in Anderson: the Assessor sets values, the Auditor handles deductions and tax sale redemption, and the Treasurer collects the money. The Auditor and Treasurer sit in the Madison County Government Center at 16 East 9th Street, Anderson, IN 46016.

  • Treasurer: takes online payments through the county's tax system, and the Treasurer's page sends assessment questions and appeals to the Assessor.
  • Auditor: homestead, over 65, blind or disabled and veteran deductions, plus deed transfers. The phone on the Auditor's page is (765) 641-9422 or (765) 641-9505.
  • Assessor: assessed values and Form 130 appeals.

The Auditor's page says online deduction filing needs the parcel number, and that filers should add an email address before submitting. Documents commonly required include an Indiana driver's license, the last five digits of the Social Security number for the filer and spouse, and an income tax return or Social Security 1099 for the over 65 deduction.

The county's state-posted documents also include the budget order for 2026, issued January 15, 2026, which holds the certified rates by fund and taxing district. Hours and holiday closures are on the county's contact page.

When is Madison County property tax due, and what are the penalties?

Madison County property tax is due May 11 and November 10 in 2026, with payment to the county Treasurer. State law sets the usual dates at May 10 and November 10 of the year after the assessment, and weekends or holidays move the date.

For late payment, the Indiana Department of Local Government Finance describes a 5 percent penalty if you pay within 30 days and owe no back taxes on the property, and 10 percent if the tax and penalty are not paid within 30 days. The Madison County pages we read did not repeat these percentages, so treat the state figures as the rule and confirm with the Treasurer.

One local detail matters for anyone who is behind. A parcel certified for tax sale cannot be paid online. The Treasurer's notice says such payments must be made in person by cashier's check, money order or cash.

The county posts its tax sale on its website. A property is eligible when it is delinquent for three or more installments, and the listings are hosted online by SRI Services. Redemption of a property sold at a tax sale or commissioners' sale goes through the Auditor's Office, not the Treasurer.

How do you appeal a Madison County assessment?

You file Form 130 in writing with the county assessing official, and it goes to the Property Tax Assessment Board of Appeals. The state fact sheet from November 2025 sets the filing deadline at June 15, with the year depending on when the county mailed its notice.

The process runs in steps:

  • An informal meeting with the assessing official.
  • A hearing before the PTABOA within 180 days of filing, with notice at least 30 days ahead.
  • An appeal to the Indiana Board of Tax Review on Form 131 if you disagree, or if the board does not decide within 180 days.

An appraisal is optional, and sales of comparable homes help. Madison County had a median home value of $147,700 in the Census figures above, so a sale price close to that range is a useful reference point for an owner who thinks the value is too high.

The state also says you can pay on last year's assessed value while an appeal is open without a penalty. A fact sheet example shows a property assessed at $200,000 this year and $100,000 last year being paid on $100,000.

What do Madison County sellers face, and how does the climate matter?

Many Madison County sellers hold older houses. The median home was built in 1965, per the Census figures above, and that age brings roof, plumbing and furnace costs.

Weather adds to it. Anderson's mean annual high is about 61.8 degrees Fahrenheit and its mean low about 43.8. Annual precipitation averages 46.3 inches, with 20.9 inches of snow. The record high is 105 and the record low is minus 24, so heating systems and roofs both work hard (Wikipedia, 2006 to 2020 normals).

The White River crosses the northern part of the city and Fall Creek runs through the south of the county. If a house sits near either, ask for the flood zone on the survey or the lender's determination. We did not find a county flood figure on the pages we read, so we do not state one.

Common reasons Madison County owners sell as-is include inherited homes, a house with tax back payments, tenant problems and repair bills that exceed what the house would bring after fixing. Checking the Auditor's tax sale list first tells you whether the parcel is already close to certification.

What are the 2026 Madison County property tax due dates?

The posted 2026 dates are May 11 and November 10. State law sets the standard installments at May 10 and November 10, and a weekend or holiday moves the date.

Where is the Madison County Treasurer?

The Treasurer is in the Madison County Government Center, 16 East 9th Street, Anderson, IN 46016. Hours and a contact list are on the county's website.

Can I pay Madison County taxes online?

Yes, the Treasurer takes online payments by electronic check, debit or credit card. A parcel certified for tax sale cannot be paid online and needs a cashier's check, money order or cash in person.

Who handles homestead deductions in Madison County?

The Auditor's Office. You need your parcel number, an Indiana driver's license and, for most filers, the last five digits of the Social Security number for you and your spouse.

What makes a Madison County property eligible for the tax sale?

The county says a property is eligible when it is delinquent for three or more installments under Indiana Code 6-1.1-24 and 6-1.1-25. The sale listings run online through SRI Services.

What is the Madison County property tax appeal deadline?

The state fact sheet gives June 15, tied to the year the tax bill is mailed or the assessment year depending on when the notice went out. Ask the Assessor to confirm which applies.

Where is Posey County, Indiana?

Posey County is the far southwestern corner of Indiana, where the Ohio River forms the southern border and the Wabash River forms the western one. It lies at the tripoint of Indiana, Kentucky and Illinois and belongs to the Evansville metropolitan area.

The county covers 419.32 square miles, with 409.57 of them land. Mount Vernon is the county seat and the largest city. Other named places include New Harmony, Poseyville, Griffin, Cynthiana, Wadesville, Blairsville, Saint Wendel and Parkers Settlement. The Black River runs southwest across the upper county to the Wabash north of New Harmony, and Rush Creek drains the middle before reaching the Wabash at Harmonie State Park.

The 2020 census counted 25,222 people. A house here is often a rural or small-town parcel, which means the assessor's land and outbuilding records matter as much as the house itself.

What is the history behind Posey County's towns?

Posey County was organized in November 1814 from parts of Gibson and Warrick counties, named for General Thomas Posey, then territorial governor. Mount Vernon became the county seat in 1825. Early settlers came mostly from the Upper South, and German immigrants followed in the middle and later 1800s.

The city of Mount Vernon had 6,493 residents in 2020, down from 6,687 in 2010 and from a peak of 7,656 in 1980. The county's two school districts, Mount Vernon MSD and North Posey County Schools MSD, split the rest of the county between them.

What drives the Posey County economy?

The Ohio River drives it. The Ports of Indiana-Mount Vernon covers about 1,200 acres on the river at 2751 Bluff Road and is described by the port authority as the state's largest port. It has more than 8,000 feet of river frontage, ten cargo terminals, and handles about 6.7 million tons a year of coal, ethanol, grain, soy products, fertilizer, steel and minerals. Around 40,000 rail cars move through it each year, and twelve companies operate there.

Mount Vernon also lists CountryMark's refinery, a SABIC plant that was formerly GE Plastics, two biofuels plants, BWX Technologies and the Evansville Western Railway among its industries. The Vectren A.B. Brown Generating Station sits about eight miles to the east.

A seller near the river and a seller on farmland face different questions: the first is dealing with a city lot, the second with acreage and outbuildings.

What should Posey County owners know about flood, wind and weather?

Low ground and open country both carry risk here. The lowest point in Indiana is where the Wabash flows into the Ohio in this county, and the highest, 590 feet, is a small rise about 1.6 miles south-southwest of Saint Wendel. The John T. Myers Locks and Dam, about 13 miles southwest of Mount Vernon, was built for navigation and flood control on the Ohio.

Tornadoes are part of the county's record. The 1925 Tri-State Tornado struck Griffin on March 18, 1925 and killed 25 people. An EF-2 tornado crossed Harmonie State Park, Blairsville and Saint Wendel on April 2, 2024.

Neither fact decides a price, but a buyer or insurer may ask about flood zone status and roof or storm damage. A house with unrepaired wind damage is a common reason owners turn to an as-is sale rather than a repair-and-list route.

When and how are Posey County property taxes paid?

Posey County mails bills in early April and collects in two installments: Monday, May 11, 2026 for spring and Tuesday, November 10, 2026 for fall. You may pay both installments together in the spring.

A payment after the due date carries a state penalty of 5 percent for the first 30 days and 10 percent after that. Payment options at the Treasurer's Office at 126 East Third Street, Room 211, in the Memorial Coliseum:

  • In person, Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.
  • Online at poseycountytax.com, where cards carry a processor convenience fee and e-checks carry a $1.50 fee.
  • The drop box in front of the Coliseum Building.
  • At United Fidelity Bank or First Bank branches listed by the county.
  • By mail, with the whole bill and a self-addressed stamped envelope if you want a receipt.

If a mortgage company pays your taxes yet you received a bill, the county says to contact the lender. Elderly and disabled deductions go through the County Auditor, not the Treasurer.

Who sets assessments in Posey County?

The Posey County Assessor sets them, and the assessment date for real property is January 1. Nancy Hoehn is listed as assessor, with a field deputy, a GIS manager and a sales disclosure deputy on the same page. Assessment notices go out in April, and the office notes that business personal property filings and exemption applications are due May 15.

Counties reassess a quarter of their parcels each year, with the statutory deadline on December 31. The county posts a GIS map where owners can look up parcels. Appeals use Indiana's Form 130, filed with the assessing official, usually by June 15. The process after that runs through an informal meeting, a county board hearing within 180 days, and then, if needed, a Form 131 petition to the Indiana Board of Tax Review within 45 days.

How does a Posey County tax sale work?

The county takes delinquent parcels to a public auction, and the 2026 notice shows the steps. The auction began at 10:00 a.m. on August 31, 2026 in the Hovey House Commissioners' Room, with the option of moving online. The list held 171 properties. The auditor and treasurer asked the court for judgment on or after August 14, 2026, and a property was pulled if its full judgment was paid before the sale.

Redemption costs 110 percent of the minimum bid within six months and 115 percent after that, plus any excess bid with 5 percent annual interest and later taxes the buyer paid. The redemption period for certificates sold in the auction ends August 31, 2027. If a property sells above the minimum bid and is not redeemed, the former owner may have a right to the surplus.

What should you do before selling a Posey County house with taxes due?

Get the exact balance first, then decide how it will be paid at closing. If you inherited the house, ask whether the bills are still addressed to the former owner, since the Treasurer's site offers a change of mailing address link.

  • Look up the parcel on the county's search and pay tool and print the bill.
  • Ask the Auditor whether any deduction ends with a sale.
  • Check the redemption deadline if the parcel was in the 2026 auction.
  • Walk the property for storm or flood damage a buyer will ask about.

A cash sale can close around those items, with the delinquent amount taken from the proceeds by the title company.

Spring was due Monday, May 11, 2026 and fall is due Tuesday, November 10, 2026. Both can be paid together in the spring.

What is the penalty for paying Posey County taxes late?

The state penalty is 5 percent for the first 30 days after the deadline and 10 percent after that, according to the Treasurer's Office.

Where is the Posey County Treasurer's Office?

It is at 126 East Third Street, Room 211, Mt. Vernon, IN 47620, in the Memorial Coliseum. The phone is (812) 838-1316 and hours are Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.

Can I get my property back after the Posey County tax sale?

Yes, by redeeming it before the period ends. For certificates sold in the 2026 auction that date is August 31, 2027, and the cost is 110 percent of the minimum bid in the first six months and 115 percent later, plus the listed extras.

Who handles tax deductions in Posey County?

The County Auditor's Office, reachable at (812) 838-1300, handles property tax deductions, including the elderly and disabled ones.

Johnson County by the numbers

Where is Johnson County, Indiana, and what is in it?

Johnson County sits directly south of Indianapolis and covers 321.79 square miles, with Franklin as the county seat and Greenwood as its largest city. It borders Marion County to the north, Shelby to the east, Bartholomew to the southeast, Brown to the southwest and Morgan to the west, and it belongs to the Indianapolis-Carmel-Anderson metro area.

The county was formed in 1823 and named for John Johnson, a justice of the Indiana Supreme Court. Wikipedia lists eight townships (Blue River, Clark, Franklin, Union, Hensley, Nineveh, Pleasant and White River) and notes that Franklin, Union and Needham townships merged in January 2022. The township and taxing district a parcel falls in decide which levies land on its bill, so look up the parcel itself instead of borrowing a neighbor's number.

Johnson County itemDetail
Total area321.79 square miles, of which 320.43 is land
County seatFranklin
Largest cityGreenwood
Formed1823
2020 census population161,765 (2025 estimate: 174,262)
Households, 202060,259, with 72.9% of occupied homes owner-occupied
Urban share, 202087.3%

How fast is Johnson County growing?

Johnson County has added people at every count since 2000. The census recorded 115,209 residents that year, 139,654 in 2010 and 161,765 in 2020, and the 2025 estimate of 174,262 is a 7.7% rise over 2020.

A county that adds people this quickly has older houses sitting close to newer ones. An owner of a dated or damaged house in Greenwood or Franklin can weigh a quick as-is sale against the cost of fixing the place up to compete with newer homes nearby.

What are the main employers and job centers in Johnson County?

Greenwood is the commercial center. In 2023 the city had 3,176 businesses employing 25,386 people, with services and retail as the largest sectors. Wikipedia names the U.S. headquarters of Endress+Hauser, Nachi America, an Amazon fulfillment center near I-65 with about 1,000 workers, and a Milwaukee Electric Tool service hub that opened in 2021. Greenwood Park Mall is the main shopping center.

Franklin leans toward manufacturing. Its listed international employers include Toyota, NSK, KYB and Mitsubishi, and Franklin College, founded in 1834, is in the city. At the south end of the county, Camp Atterbury is an Indiana National Guard training post that spans parts of Johnson, Bartholomew and Brown counties and covers roughly 30,000 acres.

  • Greenwood: retail, services, distribution and light industry along the I-65 corridor
  • Franklin: automotive and machinery suppliers, a college and the county government
  • Camp Atterbury: military training with a long history, from World War II onward

Sellers who have a job change, a transfer or a relocation behind the sale often have a closing date to hit, and a county with this mix of employers sees plenty of that.

Which school districts and roads serve Johnson County homes?

Greenwood is served by three public school corporations: Greenwood Community, Clark-Pleasant Community and Center Grove Community. Franklin Community Schools covers nearly all of Franklin, and a small northern slice of the city belongs to Clark-Pleasant. A bill for a house in one district carries a different school levy than a house in another, even when they are a few blocks apart.

I-65 has three exits on Greenwood's east side, and Exit 97 uses a diverging diamond layout. I-69 has two exits just west of the city, and U.S. 31 and State Road 135 run north to south. Franklin sits on I-65 and U.S. 31, Access Johnson County provides local bus service, and Indianapolis International Airport is roughly 28 miles northwest of Franklin. Greenwood is about 11 miles south of downtown Indianapolis.

Do floods or cold snaps affect Johnson County houses?

Yes, flooding is part of the county's recent history. In 2008, Canary Creek, Hurricane Creek and Young's Creek flooded Franklin and damaged or destroyed more than 100 homes. The city later bought many of those properties and turned them into green space for its parks system.

Winter cold is the other factor. The coldest temperature ever recorded in Indiana, minus 36 degrees Fahrenheit, was measured in New Whiteland on January 19, 1994. A house with failing pipes, an old furnace or a leaking roof can be a real expense to fix before listing. Selling as-is to a cash buyer means the seller does not have to make those repairs first.

Who handles property tax, deeds and zoning in Johnson County?

Four county offices cover most of what a seller needs, and they all keep Monday through Friday hours. The list below comes from the county's department page.

OfficePhoneWhat it covers
Assessor(317) 346-4701Assessed values, deductions and appeals
Auditor(317) 346-4310Tax bills, mailing address changes, deduction processing
Treasurer(317) 346-4330Collecting installments
Recorder(317) 346-4385Recording deeds and mortgages
Planning and Zoning(317) 346-4350Zoning and building questions

The county also runs a public mapping site at jcmaps.org, which helps when you want to check a parcel's boundaries or neighbors. The Johnson County department directory has current contacts.

How did Indiana's 2025 law change Johnson County tax bills?

Senate Enrolled Act 1 of 2025 reshaped the homestead deductions, and the Department of Local Government Finance has published the schedule. For taxes payable in 2026 the standard homestead deduction is $48,000. It steps down to $40,000 for taxes payable in 2027, $30,000 in 2028, $20,000 in 2029 and $10,000 in 2030, and it ends after that.

The supplemental deduction moves the other way, rising from 40% in 2026 to 46% in 2027 and 52% in 2028. A new supplemental homestead credit equals the lesser of 10% of the liability or $300, with no separate application. The old over-65 deduction became an over-65 credit of up to $150, with income limits of $60,000 for a single filer and $70,000 for joint filers, and the application is due by January 15 of the year taxes are first payable.

Homestead deductions go with an owner-occupant, so a bill can change after a sale. Indiana also caps bills as a share of gross assessed value: 1% for homesteads, 2% for other residential and agricultural land, and 3% for other property, according to the state's Tax Bill 101 page.

How do I appeal a Johnson County assessment?

You file Form 130 with the local assessing official. The county's own appeals page says you can only appeal the current year's assessed value this way, and it lists the steps: an informal conference with the assessor, a review by the county Property Tax Assessment Board of Appeals if the appeal is denied, then the Indiana Board of Tax Review and the Indiana Tax Court.

State guidance puts the filing deadline at June 15, either of the assessment year (when the notice goes out before May 1) or of the year the treasurer mails the bill (when it goes out later). The board must hold its hearing within 180 days of filing. The state does not require an appraisal. Evidence can include a recent sale, comparable sales, an offer to buy or an appraisal.

  • Wrong owner, a missing deduction, a clerical mistake or a wrong property description count as objective errors and go on page 2 of Form 130, for up to three years of assessments
  • A refund request also needs Form 17-T
  • While an appeal is pending, you may pay on the prior year's assessment without penalty

What happens to unpaid property tax when a Johnson County house is sold?

Unpaid tax stays with the parcel, and it is usually paid out of the sale proceeds at closing. Penalties keep growing until then: the state adds a further 10% on unpaid amounts the day after each installment's due date in years after the first delinquency, and unpaid taxes can lead to a tax sale.

Before a deed goes to the county auditor, all parties to the conveyance must sign a sales disclosure form, and under Indiana law the form first goes to the county assessor for review. The auditor then processes it and sends it back to the assessor, who keeps it for five years. The rule covers deeds and contracts of sale for value, plus compulsory transfers from foreclosure, divorce, court order or probate.

After the sale, the former owner can ask the Auditor to redirect future bills. The county's change-of-mailing-address form can be mailed to 86 W Court St, Franklin, emailed to the auditor or faxed to (317) 736-7021, and it covers up to five parcels.

How does a cash sale work for a Johnson County house with tax due?

A cash buyer prices the house as it stands, and the closing agent can usually pay any tax owed from the proceeds, so the seller does not have to clear the balance first. The process is the same whether the house is in Greenwood, Franklin or the townships around them.

  • Share the address and condition, including any back taxes or liens
  • Receive a written cash offer you can accept or decline
  • Pick a closing date that fits the move or the estate timeline
  • Sign at the title company, which records the deed with the Recorder

More questions about Johnson County, IN Property Tax Guide

What are the property tax due dates in Johnson County?

Where is Elkhart County and how is it laid out?

Elkhart County sits in northern Indiana on the Michigan line, in the area people call Michiana. Goshen is the county seat, and Elkhart is the largest city. The county covers about 468 square miles, roughly 20 miles east of South Bend and 150 miles north of Indianapolis.

Six incorporated places share the map: Elkhart, Goshen, Middlebury, Nappanee, Bristol and Wakarusa. It borders seven counties, including Cass and St. Joseph in Michigan.

Water shapes the layout. The St. Joseph River is the main waterway. The Elkhart River enters east of Millersburg, passes through Goshen and Dunlap, and joins the St. Joseph in the city of Elkhart. A house near either river or on Simonton Lake carries different drainage and insurance questions than a farm parcel near Nappanee.

What does the RV industry mean for Elkhart County home sellers?

The recreational vehicle business is the biggest swing factor in the county's household budgets. Elkhart County is known as the RV Capital of the World, and the city of Elkhart opened its first RV factory in 1934. By 1949 the city was already using that nickname.

A 2016 Indianapolis Business Journal report put numbers on the swings. Manufacturing, which covers RV makers and their suppliers, held 49.6% of county jobs in April 2006 (66,300 of 133,500). By April 2009 the share was 38.4% (37,000 of 96,200). By April 2016 it had climbed back to 46% (57,900 of 125,800). Unemployment peaked at 18.9% in March 2009 and stood at 3.9% in April 2016. These figures are a decade old, so treat them as a picture of the pattern and not a current reading.

An Indiana University economist quoted in that report described the county economy as resting on an essentially discretionary product. Local officials said many suppliers had diversified, though efforts to bring in non-RV employers had limited success.

Other employers fill in the picture. Elkhart is known for band instruments and hosts Elkhart Brass and NIBCO, and Goshen's industry centers on RV and automotive work, with names such as Benteler, Dutchmen and Keystone. When plant hours drop, a property tax installment is one of the first bills to slip, which is how many owners here end up selling with taxes due.

How is property tax set in Elkhart County?

Indiana splits the job among several county offices, and Elkhart County follows that pattern. The assessor sets values and hears appeals. The auditor applies tax cap credits to each bill. The treasurer sends bills and collects payment. Rates come from the local taxing units on your parcel, such as the county, a city or town, and a school corporation.

The state's circuit breaker caps limit the bill as a share of gross assessed value. They do not change the local tax rate. If a homestead with a $100,000 gross assessed value would owe $2,100, the auditor credits $1,100 and the owner pays $1,000.
