To get the 1% homestead cap you must hold the homestead standard deduction. A homestead covers the dwelling, a garage and up to one acre of surrounding land. For the many rural lots in Elkhart County that run larger than an acre, the extra land falls into the 2% class. The state posts each county's budget order every January, and Elkhart County's 2026 order was issued January 15, 2026 on the state's county page.

How does the county reassess houses?

Elkhart County reviews roughly a quarter of its parcels each year, so a different set of townships gets a fresh look every cycle. The assessor's 2025 ratio study narrative describes the 2024 phase. Baugo, Benton and Cleveland townships had residential and agricultural property reviewed, Concord had most districts reviewed in all classes, and York had commercial and exempt parcels reviewed.

The study used sales from January 1 to December 31, 2024. It treats improved residential property one township at a time because each had enough sales. A land order sent to the county board on December 3, 2024 took effect January 1, 2025.

  • Each sales disclosure form is checked through phone contacts, aerial maps, field visits, MLS records and CoStar.
  • Permits for all trades go into the county's assessment system. Elkhart, Goshen and Nappanee process their own permits, and the county handles the rest.

How do I appeal an Elkhart County assessment?

You file a Form 130 with the county assessor, one form per parcel. The deadline is June 15. Which June 15 depends on when the Form 11 assessment notice was mailed: if it went out before May 1, the deadline falls in that assessment year, and if it was mailed on or after May 1, the deadline falls in the year the tax bill is mailed. If no notice was sent, the tax bill counts as the notice.

After filing, the assessor schedules an informal meeting to compare information. The county Property Tax Assessment Board of Appeals must then hold a hearing within 180 days of your filing, and it must give you at least 30 days of written notice. A continuance request needs good cause and must be filed at least 10 days ahead. Skipping the hearing without a request can bring a $50 penalty.

If you disagree with the result, or the board says nothing within 180 days, you can file Form 131 with the Indiana Board of Tax Review. Further review goes to the Indiana Tax Court and then the Indiana Supreme Court. While an appeal is pending you may pay on the prior year's assessment without penalty. If you pay less than that amount, the unpaid part is delinquent. The state's appeals fact sheet lays out each step.

What happens if I sell an Elkhart County house with tax due?

Unpaid property tax does not stop a sale, but a title company will want it settled at closing, normally from the seller's proceeds.

The state's penalty rules explain why waiting costs more. Under Indiana Code 6-1.1-37-10, a late payment draws a 5% penalty if it comes within 30 days of the due date and the parcel has no earlier delinquency. In other cases the penalty is 10%. A further 10% of the unpaid principal is added the day after each later installment date. The extra 10% applies only to the tax itself, so it does not compound on earlier penalties. Payments go first to the tax and then to penalties.

  • Ask the treasurer for a current payoff before you list or accept an offer.
  • Ask the title company whether spring and fall installments are both included in the payoff.
  • File the sales disclosure form that Indiana requires with the county. A 2021 state memo said a sale closing by December 31 can qualify the buyer for a homestead deduction the next year, and the disclosure form can serve as the application. Confirm the current dates.

What should a seller know about weather and flooding here?

Northern Indiana weather is harder on roofs and basements than the average Midwest address. Goshen's averages run from a January low near 17 degrees to a July high near 85. Record lows reached minus 24 in January 1984 and the record high was 102 in June 1988. In the city of Elkhart, snowfall averages about 74 inches a year.

Flooding has a recorded history. In February 2018 the Elkhart River in Goshen rose to a record 13.2 feet after heavy rain and snowmelt. More than 300 structures were damaged and some residents had to evacuate.

Tornadoes are part of the record too. On April 11, 1965, storms hit the area, and Elkhart County recorded 55 of the state's 137 storm deaths. Sellers who have repaired water or storm damage should keep the paperwork.

Which schools, roads and neighborhoods affect a sale?

Buyers and sellers in Elkhart County usually name the school corporation before they name a street. Elkhart Community Schools serves most of the city of Elkhart. Concord Community Schools covers the southeast side of Elkhart and northwest Goshen, and Baugo Community Schools covers the southwest side. Goshen Community Schools serves most of Goshen, with small parts covered by Middlebury, Concord and WaNee.

  • The Indiana Toll Road runs along the northern edge, with exits at Elkhart, Bristol and Middlebury.
  • U.S. 20 follows the southern edge of Elkhart as the St. Joseph Valley Parkway. U.S. 6, 33 and 131 also cross the county.
  • Amtrak's Lake Shore Limited and Capitol Limited stop at Elkhart, and the Interurban Trolley connects Goshen, Elkhart and Dunlap.

Historic areas matter for older houses. Goshen's historic district, listed on the National Register in 1983, centers on the county courthouse.

Start with the county treasurer for bills and payments and the county assessor for values and appeals. The treasurer's office is in the county building in Goshen, and the due dates and hours appear in the guide above. The state information center at 1-800-457-8283 also takes general property tax questions.

When is the deadline to appeal an assessment in Elkhart County?

The deadline is June 15, filed on Form 130 with the county assessor. The year depends on when the Form 11 notice was mailed, before or after May 1. File a separate petition for each parcel.

Can I sell my Elkhart County house if I owe back taxes?

Yes. The title company pays the unpaid tax and penalties from your proceeds at closing, so the amount comes off what you receive. Get a payoff figure from the treasurer first so you know the number.

Why did my Elkhart County bill change when my value went up?

The circuit breaker caps limit the bill to 1% of gross assessed value for a homestead, 2% for other residential and farmland, and 3% for nonresidential property. Without the homestead deduction you do not get the 1% cap.

Does a flood or storm repair affect the sale of a house in Elkhart County?

It can. Buyers and inspectors look at past water damage, so keep receipts and permits. The Elkhart River reached a record 13.2 feet in February 2018, and local drainage and basement history is part of most inspections.

Boone County by the numbers

Where is Boone County, Indiana, and how is it laid out?

Boone County sits near the middle of Indiana, northwest of Indianapolis, with Lebanon as the county seat. The county runs about 24 miles east to west and 17.5 miles north to south, and covers 423.25 square miles, almost all of it land.

Its neighbors are Clinton County to the north, Hamilton to the east, Marion to the southeast, Hendricks to the south and Montgomery to the west. Sugar Creek drains the west side, Big Raccoon Creek the southwest and Eagle Creek the southeast. The highest ground is a small hill, 984 feet above sea level, about two miles northeast of Lebanon.

For a seller, the layout matters because the county is really two housing markets under one tax office. The southeast corner is suburban Zionsville, about 15 miles northwest of downtown Indianapolis. The rest is Lebanon, smaller towns and farm country, where about two thirds of the land has been cultivated.

How did Boone County get started?

The legislature created Boone County on April 1, 1830, and it was organized in 1831. It was named for the frontiersman Daniel Boone, and Jamestown served as the first county seat before Lebanon was chosen as the permanent one.

Lebanon itself was established on April 30, 1830. A pioneer reportedly picked the name because a stand of hickory trees reminded him of the Biblical cedars of Lebanon. The first post office opened in 1832, the community became a town in 1853 and a city in 1875.

Zionsville has a different story. It was laid out in 1852 when the railroad was extended to the site and was named for settler William Zion. It incorporated in 1866, and the old rail corridor is now the Big-4 Rail Trail.

What does the Boone County economy look like?

Boone County combines agriculture, manufacturing, distribution and fast-growing technology projects, with Lebanon at the center of most of them. Large employers in Lebanon include the Lebanon Community School Corporation, the U.S. headquarters of Festool and Skjodt-Barrett, and plants run by Hendrickson International, DS Smith, Kuraray, Kauffman Engineering, Maplehurst Bakeries and D-A Lubricant Company.

Distribution centers there serve CNH Parts and Services, Subaru of America, Continental Tire the Americas and Hachette Book Group USA. Witham Health Services runs medical facilities in the city.

The biggest change is the LEAP Research and Innovation District, which covers more than 9,000 acres set aside for technology and manufacturing. Eli Lilly plans a $9 billion facility there to make active ingredients for tirzepatide, with production slated to begin in late 2026. When the district is complete it is expected to employ around 50,000 people.

Projects of that size pull on local housing in two directions. Some owners expect strong demand and wait. Others, especially heirs, landlords and owners with deferred repairs, would rather sell now and skip the preparation. Both groups still owe the same tax bill until closing.

How do Boone County property tax payments work?

Boone County property tax is paid to the county treasurer in two equal installments, due May 10 and November 10 under Indiana law. The state tax calendar lists the 2026 dates as May 11 and November 10, because May 10 fell on a Sunday.

The treasurer's office is on the second floor of the county courthouse in downtown Lebanon, open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., and closed on legal holidays and Election Day. Treasurer Nikki Baldwin can be reached at 765-482-2880.

  • In person: cash, personal checks, cashier checks, certified checks and money orders. Cards are accepted only online.
  • By mail: payable to Boone County Treasurer, 209 Courthouse Square, Lebanon, IN 46052. The envelope must carry a post office postmark by the due date, and a postage meter date does not count.
  • Online and phone: through the county's payment portal or 1-877-886-1892. Cards cost 2.95% with a $1.95 minimum. An ACH payment has a flat $0.95 fee.

The treasurer warns against paying by bank bill pay check, because those envelopes usually do not receive a post office postmark. If you are selling, pay the bill directly or give the title company a copy of it.

How does a property tax appeal work in Boone County?

You start a Boone County appeal by filing Form 130 with the Assessor's Office. For 2026, the county mailed assessment notices (Form 11) on April 28 and set the appeal deadline at June 15, 2026, printed at the top of the notice.

Before appealing, check your property record card. If it lists the wrong square footage, bathroom count, outbuildings or basement, the county offers a separate correction of error. Filing is allowed by email to assessmentappeal@co.boone.in.us, by mail or in person, and you should attach evidence. Someone other than the owner or a family member needs a signed power of attorney.

  1. The Assessor reviews your appeal after the deadline and contacts you for a preliminary hearing.
  2. If you cannot agree, the Property Tax Assessment Board of Appeals (PTABOA) hears the case, usually on a Wednesday, with notice by mail.
  3. You get a Form 115 with the board's decision.
  4. If you disagree, file Form 131 with the Indiana Board of Tax Review and send the Assessor a copy.
  5. After that decision you can seek review in the Indiana Tax Court.

The county warns that an appeal can leave your value higher, lower or unchanged. State guidance says the PTABOA hearing must occur within 180 days of filing, with at least 30 days of notice. See the Boone County Assessor appeal page for current forms.

What happens to taxes and deductions when a Boone County house sells?

Indiana requires a sales disclosure form signed by the buyer and seller before the deed is filed with the county auditor. The county assessor reviews it first, and each parcel needs its own form, with a single exception for contiguous parcels inside one taxing district.

Taxes are billed in arrears, so a spring or fall installment can fall due around your closing date. Title companies normally split the bill between buyer and seller by closing date, which you should confirm with your closing agent.

The homestead deduction also changes hands. Under the version of the statute we reviewed, the standard deduction is 60% of assessed value, up to $48,000 for assessments after 2022, and a new owner who buys after the assessment date can qualify by filing the statement or a sales disclosure form with the assessor by December 31 of the purchase year. The statute was amended effective January 1, 2025, so check with the Auditor for the current figure.

What if Boone County property tax goes unpaid?

A late payment adds a penalty under Indiana law. Paying within 30 days of the due date adds 5% of the delinquent tax if there is no earlier delinquency on the parcel. In every other case the penalty is 10%.

Later installments can bring additional 10% penalties, and the penalties apply to the principal owed. Payments go first to the tax and then to the penalty. Past that point the parcel can be offered at a county tax sale, and Indiana owners generally have one year to redeem. Confirm timing with the Boone County Treasurer before assuming any date.

A house with a delinquent bill can still be sold. The unpaid tax and penalty are settled from the proceeds at closing, which is one reason sellers with several years of back tax often prefer a direct cash sale over listing.

What do Boone County sellers usually run into?

Most Boone County sellers face one of a few situations: a house that needs work, an inherited property, a tenant, or a timing problem. In Zionsville the median owner-occupied home value was reported at $406,800 in the 2016 to 2020 American Community Survey.

  • Check your Form 11 value against what you would accept in a sale.
  • Pull the property record card and fix any errors before they affect a buyer's review.
  • Keep the latest tax bill, mortgage payoff and any estate papers ready.
  • Ask the treasurer for the current balance before scheduling a closing.

If you want to skip repairs, showings and appraisal delays, a cash offer for a Boone County house can close on your timeline, with tax proration handled at the title company.

Boone County property taxes are due in two equal installments on May 10 and November 10 under Indiana law. In 2026 the state calendar listed May 11 and November 10, since May 10 was a Sunday. Mailed payments must be postmarked by the due date.

Where do I pay Boone County property tax in person?

You pay at the Boone County Treasurer's office on the second floor of the courthouse in downtown Lebanon. It is open Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., except legal holidays and Election Day. Cash, checks, cashier checks and money orders are accepted in person, and cards are online only.

What is the deadline to appeal a Boone County assessment?

The 2026 deadline was June 15, 2026, and notices were mailed April 28. File Form 130 with the Boone County Assessor, by email, mail or in person. Check the date printed on your own Form 11 each year.

How much is the late penalty on Indiana property tax?

The penalty is 5% of the delinquent amount if you pay within 30 days of the due date and have no earlier delinquency on the parcel. Otherwise it is 10%. Additional 10% penalties can attach to later installments.

Can I sell a Boone County house with unpaid property tax?

Yes, you can sell a Boone County house with taxes still owed. The balance, plus any penalty, is paid from your proceeds at closing. Ask the treasurer for an exact payoff before the closing date.

Where is Floyd County and what is the land like?

Part of the county sits in the Knobs, one of the hilliest parts of Indiana, with dry ridgetops and wet ravines. Clark, Harrison and Washington counties lie to the northeast, west and northwest. What is New Albany's history, and why does it matter for sellers?

New Albany was once the largest city in Indiana, and its old building stock shows it. Three Scribner brothers from New York founded the town in July 1813. The city held the top spot from 1816 until 1860, when Indianapolis passed it.

Shipbuilding and steamboats drove the early economy, and the steamboat trade ended by 1870. American Plate Glass Works opened in 1865 and employed up to 2,000 people before moving in 1893. Plywood and veneer manufacturing came next. The Scribner House, built in 1814, still stands, and Main Street holds late 19th century mansions from the shipbuilding years.

The Culbertson Mansion, a French Second Empire home, is now an Indiana state memorial, and the Town Clock Church was a stop on the Underground Railroad. Older homes near downtown share the county with new construction, which the county's assessment study says increased in 2024.

Income data shows why some owners fall behind. The 2023 median household income in New Albany was $54,152, against $69,477 statewide, and the poverty rate was 18.4%, against 12.3% for Indiana.

What flood and storm history should Floyd County sellers know?

Floyd County's biggest weather risk is the Ohio River. In January 1937 the river reached 60.8 feet at New Albany, and most of the town stood under water for nearly three weeks. Afterward New Albany became the first city in the region to build flood walls, and Louisville and Clark County later used its walls as models.

A tornado on March 23, 1917 killed at least 46 people on the north side of the city. The Knobs bring their own terrain, with dry ridgetops and wet ravines, so a hillside lot deserves a close look at drainage before you list.

  • Ask your insurer whether the parcel is in a mapped flood zone before you list.
  • Keep repair records for any basement or foundation water work.
  • Expect buyers to ask about roof age on older New Albany houses.

Who handles property tax in Floyd County?

Three offices share the work, and all three are in New Albany. The treasurer collects, the assessor values and the auditor handles rates, calculations and deduction forms. First Harrison Bank and Stock Yards Bank no longer do. A bill reprint costs $1.

The assessor's office also handles property transfers and splits, new construction, sales disclosures and the plat room. The auditor's page links the homestead, over 65 and mortgage deduction forms on the state's site.

How does Floyd County value a house?

Tyler Technologies prepared Floyd County's 2025 ratio study, which tests how close assessed values come to sale prices. The study used sales from January 1 to December 31, 2024. It describes sales as strong in the first half of 2024 and slower in the second half, with prices staying high. New construction rose.

Form 11, the notice of assessment, is mailed by April 30 each year. The assessor's page says appeals are due June 15 on Form 130, and the county appeals board lists three members. An error such as a removed garage or wrong square footage can be corrected on page 1 and section III of page 2 of the same form.

How do tax caps and appeals work for a Floyd County seller?

The state caps tax at 1% of gross assessed value for a homestead and 2% for other residential property and farmland. Nonresidential property and personal property are capped at 3%. You need the homestead standard deduction to get the 1% cap, and the homestead covers the house, a garage and up to one acre.

The appeal process runs on state timelines. After you file Form 130, the assessor meets with you informally, and the appeals board must hold a hearing within 180 days. You get at least 30 days of written notice. A written continuance request is due 10 days before the hearing. If the board disagrees with you or does not decide in 180 days, you can take the case to the Indiana Board of Tax Review on Form 131.

If you appeal, you may pay on last year's assessment while the case is pending. Paying less than that amount makes the installment delinquent, and penalties apply.

What happens in a Floyd County tax sale?

A county tax sale offers parcels with delinquent taxes to bidders. The treasurer's page describes Floyd County's sale as fully online. Bidders register at sriservices.com, and parcel details are on lowtaxinfo.com/floydcounty. The page gives October 15, 2026 as the sale date.

An owner who wants a parcel off the list has to pay the treasurer directly. For parcels eligible for the sale, the page says online and credit card payments are not accepted, so payment must be cash in exact change or certified funds. The auditor's page lists tax sale notices, tax sale appeals, records of sale and deeds.

The state penalty rules show how the debt grows before a sale. A late payment draws 5% if made within 30 days and no earlier delinquency exists, and 10% in other cases. A later installment date adds another 10% of the unpaid principal. Payments are applied to the tax first and penalties second. A seller who closes before the sale date normally clears the whole amount through the title company.

What do roads, schools and local services look like?

Floyd County's road network ties into Louisville. I-265 forms the northern edge of New Albany, and I-64 was built through the city in 1961, which led to the Sherman Minton Bridge. A rail and road link to Kentucky opened in 1886. Highway 150 runs near Mount Saint Francis in Floyds Knobs.

The New Albany-Floyd County Consolidated School Corporation runs the public schools. New Albany High School opened in 1853 as the state's first public high school. Indiana University Southeast sits on the northern edge of the city, and the Duncan Tunnel, finished in 1881 between New Albany and Edwardsville, is the longest in Indiana at 4,311 feet.

The Floyd County Treasurer collects it, and the office is in New Albany. Call (812) 948-5477, option 4 for tax payments, to confirm the right address first.

When is the appeal deadline in Floyd County?

June 15, on Form 130 filed with the Floyd County Assessor. Notices of assessment are mailed by April 30.

Can a Floyd County house be sold with back taxes owed?

Yes. The title company pays the back tax and penalties from the sale proceeds at closing. Ask the treasurer for the current balance so you know what to expect.

How much is the late penalty in Floyd County?

It is 5% if you pay within 30 days of the due date and have no earlier delinquency, and 10% in other cases. State law adds another 10% of the unpaid tax at later installment dates.

Does the Ohio River affect selling a house in Floyd County?

It can. The river forms the county's southern edge and flooded most of New Albany in 1937. A buyer or lender may ask about flood zone status and insurance for homes near the water.

The Indiana Toll Road carries I-80 and I-90 across the county, and US 6, US 12 and US 20 add east-west routes. How does lake-effect weather affect houses in LaPorte County?

Winters are long and snowy. La Porte averages about 65 inches of snow a year, mostly from December through February, and about 42.5 inches of precipitation. Average January lows are near 12 degrees, the record low is minus 28 from January 1977, and the record high is 104 from June 1988.

Snow load, ice dams and frozen pipes are the practical concerns for owners of older houses. Michigan City's summers are warm and humid, with frequent thunderstorms. If a roof or furnace is near the end of its life, a cash buyer takes that on as part of the purchase.

The standard homestead deduction is $48,000 for taxes payable in 2026, steps down to $40,000, $30,000, $20,000 and $10,000 in the following years, and ends with the 2030 assessment date. The supplemental deduction grows from 40% in 2026 to 62% in 2030 and 66.7% from 2031.

Howard County by the numbers

Where is Howard County, Indiana, and which towns does it include?

Howard County is in north central Indiana, and Kokomo is both the county seat and its largest city. The county covers 293.92 square miles, almost all of it land, and touches Miami County to the north, Grant to the east, Tipton to the south, Clinton to the southwest, Carroll to the west and Cass to the northwest.

Beyond Kokomo, the communities people name most often are Greentown, Russiaville and Indian Heights, along with the unincorporated community of Cassville. Wildcat Creek and the Kokomo (Wildcat Creek) Reservoir are the county's best-known water features.

Indiana organized the county in 1844 as Richardville County. It was renamed in 1846 for U.S. Representative Tilghman Howard. About 74 percent of residents live in areas counted as urban.

What do Kokomo's employers mean for people who own houses here?

Manufacturing, and automotive work in particular, is the backbone of local employment. Kokomo grew up around natural gas and railroads, and Elwood Haynes test-drove an early automobile here in 1894.

The employers named in the Wikipedia article on Kokomo give a sense of scale:

  • Stellantis Kokomo Transmission Plant, listed at 3,583 employees
  • Indiana Transmission Plants I and II, listed at 2,439 employees
  • Kokomo Casting Plant, listed at 1,281 employees

Those headcounts are the figures the article reports, so treat them as approximate. Many households here depend on a handful of plants, which makes local hiring and plant news matter to housing demand.

What weather and storm history should Howard County sellers know?

Kokomo has a humid continental climate, with about 44.4 inches of precipitation and 34.1 inches of snow in an average year (1991 to 2020 normals). January afternoons average roughly 32.5 degrees and July afternoons roughly 83.7 degrees.

Tornadoes are part of the local record. An F4 tornado struck the southern part of Kokomo on April 11, 1965, killed 25 people in the area and heavily damaged the Chrysler transmission plant and several schools. Two tornadoes hit the north side on April 20, 2004. On August 24, 2016, an EF3 tornado damaged about 1,000 homes on the south side and destroyed 80.

If you own a house with old storm damage, a roof near the end of its life or a repair that was never finished, that condition shows up in an appraisal and in a buyer's inspection.

Which offices handle property tax in Howard County?

Three offices in the Howard County Administration Center, 220 North Main Street in Kokomo, share the work: the assessor sets value, the auditor keeps the deduction and tax sale records, and the treasurer collects the money. All three list weekday hours of 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.

How do Indiana's caps and deductions change a Howard County bill?

The rate is only part of the picture, because Indiana limits what a parcel can owe as a share of its gross assessed value. The state's circuit breaker caps are:

  • 1 percent for a homestead that receives the homestead standard deduction
  • 2 percent for other residential property, which includes single-family houses that are not homesteads and buildings with two or more dwelling units
  • 2 percent for agricultural land and 3 percent for nonresidential and personal property

The homestead standard deduction is shrinking on a schedule set by the 2025 legislation. The Department of Local Government Finance memo lists $48,000 for the 2025 assessment date, $40,000 for 2026, $30,000 for 2027 and $0 from 2030 on. A supplemental homestead deduction grows over the same years, starting at 40 percent for taxes payable in 2026 and reaching 66.7 percent in 2031.

The Howard County Auditor says a homestead application must be completed and dated by December 31, and that you do not need to reapply each year unless the property is sold, the title changes or the contract is paid off. For a buyer, that means the seller's deduction does not carry over automatically.

How do you appeal a Howard County assessment?

You start with a Form 130 filed with the assessing official, one petition per parcel. The deadline is June 15 of the year tied to the notice: if the county mails Form 11 before May 1, it is June 15 of that assessment year; otherwise it is June 15 of the year the treasurer mails the bill.

After filing, the assessor schedules a preliminary informal meeting and reports the result to the county board. The board must hold a hearing within 180 days of the petition and mail notice at least 30 days ahead. If you disagree with the decision, or no decision arrives in 180 days, you can file Form 131 with the Indiana Board of Tax Review.

Two details help owners. The assessor carries the burden of proof if the value rose more than 5 percent over the prior assessment date, unless the jump came from renovation, new improvements or a change in use. And while an appeal is pending, you may pay on the previous year's assessment without penalty until it is resolved.

When is Howard County property tax due, and what does late cost?

The 2026 installments are due May 11 and November 10. Late payments carry a 5 percent charge if paid within 30 days (on a parcel with no back taxes), and the charge rises to 10 percent of the unpaid tax after that.

Indiana bills a year behind. The bill you pay in 2026 reflects ownership and value as of January 1 of the prior year, which is why a mid-year closing can leave a buyer paying a prorated share of the seller's arrears. Your closing agent sets the exact split.

The treasurer takes payments online through InvoiceCloud, at four named local banks and in a drop box to the right of the Administration Center entrance.

What happens when Howard County taxes go unpaid?

Parcels with delinquent taxes go to an annual tax sale. The 2026 advertisement listed 460 parcels for October 27, 2026, with a 10:00 a.m. start in the Commissioners' Meeting Room and a possible move to an online auction.

A property cannot sell for less than the delinquent taxes and special assessments, the taxes due in the sale year, penalties, $25 for postage and publication, and related county costs. The owner can still redeem after the sale:

  • 110 percent of the minimum bid if redeemed within six months, or 115 percent after that
  • Plus any overbid amount and 5 percent yearly interest on it, plus taxes the buyer paid afterward
  • For certificates sold at the 2026 sale, the redemption period ends October 27, 2027; certificates struck to the county may end February 24, 2027

Defenses had to be filed with the Howard County Circuit Court before October 9, 2026.

What should you gather before selling a Howard County house with tax due?

Collect the paper that shows exactly what is owed before you talk to any buyer. The county treasurer can tell you the amount due on a parcel, and a closing agent pays it from proceeds.

  • Any Form 11 assessment notice and any Form 130 you filed
  • Whether the parcel appears on the certified tax sale list
  • Records of weed cut, demolition or nuisance liens the treasurer has placed
  • Your homestead deduction approval, if you claimed one

The office phone numbers above are the right place to confirm any figure before you rely on it.

The Howard County Treasurer, at 220 North Main Street, Room 226 in Kokomo, collects property tax and can be reached at 765-456-2213. The assessor sets value and the auditor handles deductions, so questions about value or a missing homestead deduction go to those offices instead.

May 11, 2026 and November 10, 2026. Partial payments are accepted, and the treasurer lists online, bank and drop box options.

What is the penalty for paying Howard County taxes late?

The state's schedule adds 5 percent for payment within 30 days of the due date on a parcel with no back taxes, and 10 percent of the unpaid tax after that.

How do I appeal my Howard County assessment?

File Form 130 with the assessor by June 15 of the year tied to your notice, one form per parcel. If the county board's decision is unsatisfactory, Form 131 goes to the Indiana Board of Tax Review.

Do I need to reapply for the homestead deduction after buying a house in Howard County?

Yes. The auditor says you reapply when a property is sold or the title changes, and the application must be completed and dated by December 31.

Can I sell a Howard County house that is on the tax sale list?

The treasurer's page says a parcel comes off the certified list when the taxes are paid, using cash, a cashier's check or a credit card. After a tax sale, the owner can still redeem during the redemption period, which for certificates sold at the 2026 sale ends October 27, 2027.

Form 11 notices had to be mailed by April 30. Owners could scan the QR code on the notice to appeal online, download Form 130, or go to the assessor's office. Smith said an appeal leads to an individual review of the property rather than the mass assessment.

Clark County by the numbers

Where is Clark County, Indiana?

Clark County is in southern Indiana on the north bank of the Ohio River, directly across from Louisville, Kentucky. Jeffersonville is both the county seat and the largest city.

The county covers 376.45 square miles, of which 372.86 is land. The terrain is low rolling hills, and the western part is cut by drainages. The highest point, 1,030 feet, is a ridge west-northwest of Henryville. Other places you will see on Clark County deeds include Clarksville, Charlestown, Sellersburg, Henryville, Marysville and Speed.

Charlestown held the county seat for decades before Jeffersonville took it back in the 1800s. Clark Regional Airport serves the county, and Jeffersonville's position across the river from Louisville gives it quick access to a much larger metro area.

What is the history of Clark County?

Clark County was formed on February 3, 1801, and named for General George Rogers Clark. Settlement began in 1783, and Clarksville, founded in 1784, was the first authorized American settlement in the Northwest Territory.

Jeffersonville grew around Fort Finney, built in 1786 near where the Kennedy Bridge stands today. Shipbuilding began there in 1819, and James Howard's shipyards started in 1832. Those yards later became Jeffboat, once the largest inland shipbuilder in the country. Jeffboat closed in 2018 after employing over 13,000 people at its peak, and the city announced plans in 2022 to redevelop the 80-acre site.

Charlestown also matters to the county story. The Indiana Arsenal, built nearby in 1940, produced smokeless powder in World War II and employed up to 20,000 workers.

What does the Clark County economy depend on?

Clark County has moved from river and heavy industry to a mix of health care, education, finance, logistics and manufacturing. Largest employers in Jeffersonville, as of 2020, included Greater Clark County Schools at about 1,600 employees and Norton Clark Hospital at about 1,500.

The older industrial base was broad. Ford Plate Glass was established in 1876, the Louisville Cement Company operated in Speed, and Colgate-Palmolive ran on the Clarksville riverfront from the 1920s until early 2008.

River Ridge sits on land from the former Indiana Army Ammunition Plant and now hosts manufacturing, aerospace, automotive, food and beverage, life sciences and logistics companies. Interstate 65 has shaped growth since the 1950s, when it encouraged subdivisions and shopping centers.

The Big Four Bridge, a former rail bridge opened for walkers and cyclists in 2014, draws about 1.5 million crossings a year and has made the Jeffersonville riverfront a destination.

Which Jeffersonville areas come up in Clark County sales?

Jeffersonville includes several areas with their own history, and a seller's parcel may sit in any of them. Port Fulton is a historic area now inside the city, where Jefferson General Hospital and the Howard Shipyards once stood. Oak Park was annexed in 2008, a move that brought the city's population to nearly 50,000.

The downtown and riverfront area holds restaurants, shops and Big Four Station plaza. The NoCo Arts and Cultural District is also in the city. The 2020 census counted 49,447 residents, up from 44,953 in 2010 and 27,362 in 2000.

That growth, much of it from annexation, means tax districts vary across city limits. Check which taxing district your parcel falls in, since the bill combines county, municipal and school levies.

How much does Ohio River flooding and severe weather matter in Clark County?

Flood and storm history is a real factor for Clark County homes. The 1937 flood covered about 90% of Jeffersonville, cut electricity and blocked access roads, and a levee failed during the event.

Wind is the other recorded hazard. The March 2 and 3, 2012 tornado outbreak heavily damaged Marysville and Henryville. A home in either area may have been rebuilt or repaired since then, so a buyer's inspector will ask for permits and repair records.

If your house sits near the river or a creek, ask your insurer about flood coverage and keep any elevation or damage paperwork.

How do Clark County property tax payments work?

Clark County taxes are paid to the county treasurer in two installments, generally due May 10 and November 10, with paper bills mailed in early April. The state due date page showed May 11 and November 10 for 2026.

The treasurer's office is at 300 Corporate Drive, Suite 105, Jeffersonville, open Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. and closed from noon to 1 p.m. The phone number is 812-285-6205. Mailed payments go to PO Box 1689, Evansville, IN 47706, and the county asks you to include Copy A or Copy B of the bill and a stamped, self-addressed envelope for a receipt.

  • Card payments: 2.25% plus $1.50 per transaction
  • E-check up to $99,999: $1.50 per transaction
  • Duplicate bill: $1.00 per parcel
  • Payment without the barcoded coupon: $1.00 per parcel

Several local banks accept payment during collection season, but only with the bill in hand, only for accounts with no delinquency, and only by the due date.

What are the Clark County property tax appeal steps?

Indiana's state deadline for a Form 130 appeal is June 15 of the year the county sends the assessment notice, or of the year the tax bill is mailed when no Form 11 is sent. You file one petition per parcel with the assessing official.

After filing, the assessor schedules an informal meeting and reports the result to the Property Tax Assessment Board of Appeals. State guidance says the board must hold its hearing within 180 days of the petition, with at least 30 days of mailed notice. A $50 penalty can apply if you skip the hearing without a valid continuance or withdrawal. If you disagree with the board, Form 131 goes to the Indiana Board of Tax Review.

We could not confirm the current Clark County assessor contact details on an official page, so call the county before the deadline.

How does a Clark County tax sale work?

Real property with delinquent taxes is offered at a tax certificate sale run by the Clark County Treasurer. A winning bidder receives a lien through a Tax Sale Certificate issued by the County Auditor.

The owner has one year from the sale date to redeem the property by paying the amounts set by Indiana Code, including interest. If it is not redeemed, the bidder may seek a tax deed. Property listings are published at sriservices.com, and the county recommends legal advice for bidders.

The late penalty before that stage is 5% of the delinquent tax if you pay within 30 days and have no earlier delinquency, and 10% otherwise.

What do Clark County sellers usually face?

Clark County sellers often face deferred repairs, inherited houses and landlord exits, and each of these carries tax questions. Here is a short checklist.

  • Complete the sales disclosure form, which Indiana requires before the deed reaches the county auditor.

  • If you claim the homestead deduction, remember that a buyer who purchases after the assessment date can claim it by December 31 of the purchase year.

What is the history of Dubois County?

Portersville was the original county seat, and the seat moved to Jasper in 1830. Jasper was founded in 1818 and platted in 1830, incorporated as a town in 1866 and as a city in 1915. Milk sickness reportedly killed as many as half of the county's residents in 1818.

Other employers named include Jasper Engines and Transmissions and the Southern Indiana Education Center. The city also hosts Vincennes University's Jasper Campus. Public schools in Jasper include Jasper High School, Jasper Middle School, Ireland Elementary and Jasper Elementary, and the Holy Trinity Catholic School campuses serve private families.

The county is part of the Jasper Micropolitan Statistical Area, which is now made up of Dubois County alone, since Pike County was removed in 2023. Huntingburg, Ferdinand and the community of Dubois are other named places in the county.

The 2020 census counted 43,637 people in Dubois County, up from 41,889 in 2010, and the 2025 estimate is 44,016. The median age is 41.2, and the county has 17,412 households. About 9.5% of residents are Hispanic or Latino, and about 52.4% live in urban areas.

Jasper had 16,703 residents in 2020, up from 15,038 in 2010 and 12,100 in 2000, which makes it the 48th largest city in Indiana. It lies within Bainbridge, Boone and Madison townships, and 98.2% of its residents live in urban areas. The county votes in Indiana's 8th congressional district.

Delaware County by the numbers

Where is Delaware County, Indiana, and what is its landscape?

Delaware County is in east central Indiana, with Muncie as both the county seat and the largest city, about 50 miles northeast of Indianapolis. The county covers 395.91 square miles, with 392.12 of them land.

The land is low rolling prairie with fertile soil. The Mississinewa River flows west through the north, and the White River runs west through the center and past Muncie. Prairie Creek Reservoir, southeast of Muncie, is managed by the city. The highest ground is a hilly area in the southeast corner. Blackford, Jay, Randolph, Henry, Madison and Grant counties surround it.

Muncie sits on the West Fork of the White River at 935 feet. Its climate is humid continental, with about 40 inches of precipitation and 25 inches of snow in a typical year, which matters to roofs, gutters and furnaces on older houses.

How did Delaware County develop?

Delaware County was authorized in 1820 and organized in 1827 on land gained through the 1818 Treaty of St. Mary's. It takes its name from the Delaware people, who settled along the White River and were moved west of the Mississippi in the 1840s.

Muncie began as a trading post renamed Muncietown and was platted as the county seat in 1827. The name was shortened in 1845, the town incorporated in 1854 and it became a city in 1865.

The natural gas boom changed everything. Indiana's first natural gas well opened in 1884, and the Ball brothers brought a glass foundry to Muncie in 1888. Iron and steel mills followed, and Kitselman Steel and Wire was the largest employer in Indiana in 1900 with 11,000 workers.

What does the Delaware County economy rely on now?

The Delaware County economy has shifted from manufacturing toward education, health care and retail. The Ball family donated the school property that became the forerunner of Ball State University, which opened in 1918, and helped fund Ball Memorial Hospital, which opened in 1929.

Newer manufacturers include Brevini Wind, which arrived in 2009, and Progress Rail, a Caterpillar subsidiary, which arrived in 2011. Growth has concentrated on the north side of Muncie, while the older industrial south side has seen less.

Residents disagree about how to read that change. Older workers tend to identify with manufacturing, while newer residents focus on education and health services. Muncie also drew national attention as the subject of the Lynds' 1929 Middletown study, and Ball State's Center for Middletown Studies continues that research.

How is Delaware County governed?

Delaware County is run by a seven-member county council and a three-member board of commissioners, and it has five circuit courts. It lies in Indiana's 5th congressional district and is part of the Muncie metropolitan area, within the larger Indianapolis, Carmel and Muncie combined statistical area.

Muncie spreads across Center, Hamilton, Harrison, Liberty and Mount Pleasant townships. The county Assessor's Office keeps property cards with some transfer history and maintains legal descriptions for parcels in Center Township. About 76.9% of county residents live in urban areas, and the median age countywide is 36.7.

How do roads and transit affect Delaware County homes?

Interstate 69 runs just west of Muncie, and U.S. Route 35 plus State Routes 3, 32, 67 and 332 also serve the city. The Cardinal Greenway rail trail runs 60 miles from Richmond to Marion through the area.

Muncie Indiana Transit System operates 14 fixed bus routes, daily except Sundays. Delaware County Regional Airport has no commercial service, and the nearest commercial airports in Fort Wayne and Indianapolis are each about 75 miles away.

When are Delaware County property taxes due, and where do I pay?

The Auditor's office is at 100 West Main Street, Room 103, Muncie, IN 47305, open Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. The phone number is 765-747-7717. The Treasurer's mailing address on file is 100 W Main St, Room 102. We could not confirm the Treasurer's current hours or payment methods on an official page, so call before you go.

  • To change the mailing address on your tax statement, go to the Auditor's office.
  • If statements are not coming in your name, contact the Plat Room at the same number.

How do you appeal a Delaware County assessment?

Indiana's Form 130 deadline is June 15 of the year the county mails the assessment notice, or of the year the tax bill goes out when no notice is sent. You file one petition for each parcel with the assessing official.

The assessor then holds an informal meeting and reports back to the Property Tax Assessment Board of Appeals. State guidance requires the hearing within 180 days of filing, with notice mailed at least 30 days ahead. If you disagree with the result, Form 131 goes to the Indiana Board of Tax Review. We did not find a Delaware County assessor page with current deadlines, so confirm with the county.

A homestead deduction can matter as much to a final bill as a lower assessed value. Under the statute we reviewed, the standard deduction is 60% of assessed value up to $48,000 for assessment dates after 2022, with a January 5 filing date. It was amended effective January 1, 2025, so verify the current rule.

What happens with a Delaware County tax sale and surplus?

When a Delaware County property is sold at a tax sale, only the owner whose property was sold can claim the surplus. Anyone else, even with a power of attorney, must petition the court.

The surplus becomes available only after the court issues a tax deed and the deed is recorded with the Delaware County Recorder's Office. Questions go to the Auditor's office at 765-747-7717.

Before that, the late penalty is 5% of the delinquent tax when paid within 30 days and no earlier delinquency exists, or 10% in other cases. Selling the house before a tax sale can avoid losing it to a certificate holder.

What do Delaware County sellers usually face?

Delaware County sellers often have older houses, inherited property or rental units. The sales disclosure form is required before a deed reaches the auditor, and each parcel needs its own form.

  • Get a payoff figure for taxes and any penalties.
  • Confirm the mailing address on the tax bill.
  • Gather estate papers if the owner has died.
  • Decide whether repairs make sense before selling.

Cash buyers can close without a lender appraisal, and the title company settles taxes from your proceeds.

More questions about Delaware County, IN Property Tax Guide

When are Delaware County property taxes due?

They are due on or before May 10 and November 10 each year, and the date shifts when it falls on a weekend or holiday. The state's 2026 calendar listed May 11 and November 10.

Where do I change the mailing address on my Delaware County tax bill?

Make the request at the Auditor's office, 100 West Main Street, Room 103, Muncie. The office is open Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. and the phone is 765-747-7717.

Who can claim surplus from a Delaware County tax sale?

Only the owner whose property was sold. Anyone else must petition the court, even with a power of attorney. Surplus is available after a tax deed is issued and recorded.

What is the deadline to appeal a Delaware County assessment?

The state deadline is June 15 of the year the notice or tax bill is mailed, on Form 130. File one petition per parcel and check your notice for the exact date.

Can I sell a Delaware County house with back taxes?

Yes. The unpaid taxes and penalties are paid from your proceeds at closing, and a cash sale can close before a tax sale happens.

Where is Owen County, Indiana?

Owen County is in southwest central Indiana, with Spencer as its seat and largest town. It covers 387.82 square miles, of which 385.29 are land, and it borders Putnam, Morgan, Monroe, Greene and Clay counties (Wikipedia).

The state authorized the county on December 21, 1818 and organized it in 1819, carving it from northern Daviess County and eastern Sullivan County. It was named for Colonel Abraham Owen, who died at the Battle of Tippecanoe in 1811. The first commissioners chose Spencer as the seat in 1820.

The county has thirteen townships: Clay, Franklin, Harrison, Jackson, Jefferson, Jennings, Lafayette, Marion, Montgomery, Morgan, Taylor, Washington and Wayne. Spencer and Gosport are the two incorporated towns. Communities such as Cataract, Coal City, Patricksburg and Freedom fill out the map.

The 2020 census counted 21,321 people in the county and 2,454 in Spencer, which sits in Washington Township and counts as part of the Bloomington metropolitan area.

What is the land and climate like in Owen County?

Owen County is low, wooded hill country cut by the White River, which enters from Monroe County and flows southwest through the lower middle of the county. The highest point is 934 feet, about two miles south of Quincy. Much of the land is still tree covered, with parts cleared for farms and towns.

The state's first park, McCormick's Creek State Park (established 1916), lies in Owen County. Owen-Putnam State Forest reaches into the county, and Cataract Falls State Recreation Area borders it.

Spencer has a humid subtropical climate, per Wikipedia. Average precipitation there is about 49.7 inches a year, with about 15.8 inches of snow. The January average low is 15 degrees Fahrenheit and the July average high is 84. The record high is 107 (July 1954) and the record low is minus 33 (January 1994).

For an Owen County house, that mix means wet springs, heavy summer humidity and real winter cold.

What do people in Owen County do for work and school?

Agriculture and wooded land use shape the county, and the sources we read describe significant land in farming, with some in urban use. We did not find an official employer list for Owen County, so we do not name specific employers.

Spencer is the hub. The Owen County Courthouse there is on the National Register of Historic Places, along with the Allison-Robinson House, the David Enoch Beem House, the Spencer Public Library and the Spencer Town Hall and Fire Station. Spencer was platted in 1820 and a post office has operated there since 1821.

Owen Valley Community High School is in Spencer and has about 980 students. It was built in 1971 from the consolidation of several smaller county schools, and its mascot is the Patriot.

Downtown Spencer hosts events such as the Apple Butter Festival and Christmas at the Square, which is relevant if you are staging or showing a house in the fall.

Who handles property tax in Owen County, and where are the offices?

Owen County property tax is split between the Assessor, the Auditor and the Treasurer, all in the Historic Courthouse at 60 S. Main Street, Spencer, IN 47460.

OfficeWhat it doesContact on the county site
AssessorSets assessed values, takes Form 130 appealsRoom 100; (812) 829-5018
AuditorHomestead, over 65 and other deductions(812) 829-5000
TreasurerBills and collects tax, runs the annual tax sale(812) 829-5011; Treasurer@owencounty.in.gov

The Treasurer's page lists hours of 8 a.m. to noon and 1 to 4 p.m., Monday to Friday, closed on legal holidays. Two county pages give different room numbers and phone numbers for the Treasurer, so call before you drive over.

The Assessor's office estimates market value in use for more than 17,000 parcels in the county. The assessment date is January 1 each year, and changes after that date generally take effect the following January 1, except for natural disaster exceptions.

When is Owen County property tax due and how can you pay?

Owen County's 2026 installments are due May 11 and November 10. Mail must be postmarked by the due date, and a postage meter date does not count as a postmark.

The Treasurer lists several ways to pay:

  • Online through the county's Municipay portal, where several parcels can be paid together.
  • By mail, with checks payable to "Treasurer of Owen County" and the parcel number in the memo line.
  • In person with cash, cashier's check, money order, personal check or card.
  • In the drop box at the north doors of the Historic Courthouse. Items in the box before midnight on the due date are timely.
  • By phone at 812-678-7599.
  • At the Spencer branch of The Peoples State Bank from November 2 through 10, 2026. Banks close earlier than the Treasurer's Office.

Card payments carry a fee of 2.25 percent with a $3.00 minimum, online or in person. An e-check online costs a flat $0.50. The Treasurer's page does not list penalty amounts. The Indiana Department of Local Government Finance describes 5 percent for payment within 30 days and 10 percent after that.

What happens at the Owen County tax sale?

Owen County's 2026 tax sale is on October 7, 2026, held online through sriservices.com. Delinquent parcels can be sold at the annual real estate tax sale, which the Treasurer's office runs.

The Treasurer's office lists delinquent tax collection among its services. A parcel owner who wants to avoid a sale has to bring the account current before the sale date, so ask the office for the exact payoff.

Since the 2026 sale date has passed, call the Treasurer at 812-829-5011 to find out whether a parcel was sold and what options remain.

For an owner behind on taxes, a sale of the house to a buyer who closes quickly is another route, since the delinquent amount comes out of the proceeds at closing through the title company.

How does an Owen County assessment appeal work?

An Owen County owner who disagrees with a value files Form 130 in writing with the Assessor. The Assessor holds a preliminary informal meeting and records the result on Form 134, signed by both sides.

The PTABOA must hold a hearing within 180 days of filing, and notice goes out at least 30 days ahead. A continuance request showing good cause is due at least 10 days before the hearing, and a request for a decision without a hearing is due at least 20 days before. A withdrawal waives the right to appeal to the Indiana Board of Tax Review.

A few cautions from the Assessor's page:

  • An appraisal is not required.
  • The PTABOA can raise an assessment based on the evidence.
  • Missing a hearing without a granted continuance can bring a $50 penalty, which is not added to the tax bill.

The state fact sheet sets the filing deadline at June 15, tied to the year the bill is mailed or the assessment year. It also says you may pay on the prior year's assessed value while the appeal is pending.

What should an Owen County seller expect?

Owen County is small, with about 21,000 residents spread over 13 townships, so a seller is dealing with a local market and local offices.

Homestead status is a practical item. The Auditor at (812) 829-5000 handles deductions, and a buyer files for their own after closing. Under the 2025 state changes, the standard homestead deduction is $40,000 for the 2026 assessment date, down from $48,000, and it steps down each year after that (Indiana DLGF memo, May 2026). A seller who has been paying on a deducted value should know the new owner's bill may be higher.

A cash sale still needs clear title and settled taxes. It skips the wait for lender financing, an appraisal and lender-required repairs.

When are Owen County property taxes due in 2026?

The Owen County Treasurer lists the spring installment as May 11, 2026 and the fall installment as November 10, 2026. Mailed payments need a postmark on or before the due date.

Where is the Owen County Treasurer's Office?

It is in the Historic Courthouse at 60 S. Main Street, Spencer, IN 47460. The county site lists hours of 8 a.m. to noon and 1 to 4 p.m., Monday to Friday.

Is there a drop box for Owen County tax payments?

Yes, at the north doors of the Historic Courthouse. Payments placed there before midnight on the due date are timely, and items after midnight are late.

When is the Owen County tax sale?

The Treasurer lists the 2026 sale for October 7, 2026, online only through sriservices.com. Call the office to ask about any parcel.

How do I appeal my Owen County assessment?

File Form 130 in writing with the Assessor. The PTABOA must hold a hearing within 180 days of filing, and you can go on to the Indiana Board of Tax Review on Form 131 if you disagree.

What fees apply to paying Owen County taxes by card?

Card payments, online or in person, cost 2.25 percent with a $3.00 minimum. An online e-check costs $0.50, according to the Treasurer's page.
